questions.stem: The official's reasoning is most vulnerable to which criticism?
choices: It treats a correlation as evidence of a causal relationship in a particular direction
It relies on a sample of countries that is too small
It assumes that all foreign investment is beneficial
It fails to define what counts as an international conference
questions.explanation: Correct: the official sees conferences and investment moving together and assumes the conferences produce the investment, when the causation plausibly runs the other way — countries investors already favor are the ones chosen as venues. Sample size is not the problem; the pattern is described as general, and a larger sample of the same correlation would license the same faulty leap. Whether foreign investment is beneficial goes to whether the goal is worth pursuing, not to whether conferences achieve it. Defining 'international conference' more tightly would sharpen the measurement without repairing the causal inference.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the ministry's conclusion?
choices: The program's administrative costs exceeded initial projections
Regional export volumes rose an average of 14 percent over the same period in countries with no such program
Some exporters were unaware the program existed
The program will require reauthorization next year
questions.explanation: Correct: if comparable countries without the program gained 14 percent while this one gained 12, the rise looks like a regional tide the program did not cause, and may even have dampened. Administrative costs running over budget speak to whether the program is worth its price, not to whether it raised exports. Exporters being unaware of it would, if anything, make a genuine 12 percent effect more impressive from fewer participants. Needing reauthorisation next year is a procedural fact with no bearing on what the six-month figures show.

questions.stem: Which of the following must be true?
choices: Country X may or may not have reduced its infant mortality below 10 per thousand
Country X will eventually reduce its infant mortality rate below 10 per thousand
Country X has reduced its infant mortality rate below 10 per thousand
Country X has not reduced its infant mortality rate below 10 per thousand
questions.explanation: Correct: prenatal care is stated as necessary for low infant mortality, not sufficient, so knowing Country X has it leaves its mortality rate entirely open. Concluding the rate is below 10 affirms the consequent — the classic error the item tests. Saying it eventually will assumes the condition guarantees the outcome on a delay, which the premise never suggests. Concluding it has not is equally unfounded: nothing rules the outcome out, and the premise is consistent with X having achieved it.

questions.stem: Which most seriously undermines the director's recommendation?
choices: Adult literacy is difficult to measure precisely
Both programs were evaluated by the same team
Program A was more expensive per participant than Program B
Program B was implemented in districts selected for their existing educational infrastructure
questions.explanation: Correct: if B's three districts were chosen for the educational infrastructure they already had, its 14-point gain reflects favorable conditions rather than a better program, and expanding it nationwide would not reproduce that result. Program A costing more per participant would strengthen the recommendation, not undermine it. A single evaluation team applies the same standard to both, which aids comparison rather than distorting it. Measurement difficulty in adult literacy affects both programs alike and so cannot explain the gap between them.

questions.stem: The historian's explanation assumes which of the following?
choices: Wartime alliances are never renegotiated after hostilities end
Time pressure during wartime negotiations produces terms that make alliances less durable
Alliance duration is the best measure of alliance effectiveness
Peacetime alliances are always negotiated by more experienced diplomats
questions.explanation: Correct: the explanation moves from a difference in negotiating conditions to a difference in how long alliances last, which holds only if the pressure actually produces terms that wear badly. Whether peacetime negotiators are more experienced is a separate hypothesis the historian does not need and does not offer. Whether wartime alliances are renegotiated afterwards is irrelevant, since the claim concerns their formation. Whether duration measures effectiveness questions why the pattern matters, but the historian is explaining the pattern, not defending its significance.

questions.stem: The minister's argument is most vulnerable to the objection that:
choices: Growth is not the only measure of economic performance
Capital controls may have been adopted precisely by countries already facing economic difficulties
The minister has a personal interest in the outcome
Some countries outside the region have adopted capital controls successfully
questions.explanation: Correct: countries reach for capital controls when already in difficulty, so slow subsequent growth may reflect the trouble that prompted the controls rather than damage the controls did — reverse causation dressed as a policy lesson. Successful adopters elsewhere would weaken the generalization slightly but leave the regional evidence standing. Noting that growth is not the only measure of performance changes the subject to what should be valued. Pointing to the minister's personal interest attacks the speaker and never engages the evidence.

questions.stem: The administrators' conclusion is most vulnerable because:
choices: The survey relies on participants' self-reported change in attitude, which may not reflect actual change
Favorable attitudes may not persist over time
78 percent is not a large enough majority
The survey did not include participants who withdrew from the program
questions.explanation: Correct: participants are being asked, after the fact, to compare their present view with a past one they can no longer consult, and they know what answer the program hopes for — so the 78 percent may record willingness to please rather than any real shift. Complaining that 78 percent is too small a majority concedes the measure and quibbles about its size. Excluding withdrawals and the durability of the attitudes are genuine limitations, but each assumes the reported change occurred; the self-report problem is that it may not have.

questions.stem: The section chief's reasoning is flawed primarily because it:
choices: Overstates the importance of social media
Relies on an unrepresentative sample of local media
Assumes that a temporal correlation establishes causation without considering other explanations
Confuses favorable mentions with favorable attitudes
questions.explanation: Correct: two things moved in the same period and the chief assumes one drove the other, without excluding a bilateral dispute, a change in outlet ownership, or a rival information campaign — any of which would explain the decline. Calling the media sample unrepresentative questions the measurement rather than the inference drawn from it. Distinguishing mentions from attitudes is a fair caution but concerns what favorable coverage signifies, not what caused it to fall. Overstating social media's importance describes a bias without identifying the reasoning error.

questions.stem: Which of the following can be properly inferred?
choices: Most states that submit reports have not ratified the convention
Submitting an annual compliance report is not sufficient to establish that a state has ratified the convention
Some states that have not ratified the convention are nonetheless required to submit reports
All states that submit reports have ratified the convention
questions.explanation: Correct: if some reporting states have not ratified, then reporting cannot by itself establish ratification — exactly what the second premise shows. Saying non-ratifiers are nonetheless required to report adds an obligation the stimulus never mentions; they may report voluntarily. Claiming all reporting states have ratified contradicts that premise outright. Claiming most reporting states have not ratified converts 'some' into a majority, and 'some' is compatible with a mere handful.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the analyst's argument?
choices: In the thirty-six unsuccessful cases, the targeted governments made no policy concessions of any kind
Sanctions regimes are typically maintained for several years
The four successful cases all involved sanctions imposed by a single country
Sanctions imposed on democratic governments succeed at a similar rate
questions.explanation: Correct: the claim is that sanctions rarely change behavior, so confirming that the thirty-six failures produced no concessions of any kind forecloses the obvious reply that partial movement went uncounted. The four successes coming from a single sanctioning country explains how they succeeded without addressing the general failure rate. A similar success rate against democracies actually weakens the argument, since it suggests regime type is not what drives the outcome. How long regimes are maintained describes their duration, not their effect.

questions.stem: The officer's conclusion is most vulnerable to the objection that:
choices: Documentation volume may be a marker of applicant circumstances rather than a cause of approval
The officer has not specified how much documentation counts as extensive
Some applicants cannot afford to obtain extensive documentation
Reviewing more documentation lengthens interviews
questions.explanation: Correct: applicants with steady employment, property and family ties naturally possess more paperwork and are also genuinely likelier to qualify, so the documents mark the circumstances rather than create the approval — advising weak applicants to bring more would not change what the paper documents. Affordability explains why some cannot comply without addressing whether compliance would help. Longer interviews are an administrative cost of the advice, not a reason it would fail. An undefined threshold for 'extensive' makes the observation imprecise but leaves the causal error untouched.

questions.stem: Which of the following follows from the commission's statement?
choices: Country Y will never become a democracy
Hyperinflation is caused by authoritarian government
Country Y is not currently transitioning to democracy
Ending hyperinflation would cause Country Y to democratize
questions.explanation: Correct: the premise rules out transitioning while hyperinflation persists, so it licenses a statement about Country Y's present situation and nothing more. Saying Y will never become a democracy ignores that hyperinflation can end. Claiming hyperinflation is caused by authoritarian government reverses and invents a causal relationship the report never asserts. Claiming that ending hyperinflation would cause democratisation treats the removal of an obstacle as a guarantee of the outcome, which the premise plainly does not support.

questions.stem: The adviser's argument depends on assuming that:
choices: Reporting quality is the primary purpose of overseas posts
The higher ratings at larger posts result from staffing levels rather than from characteristics of those posts
Washington consumers rate cables accurately
All posts produce cables on similar subjects
questions.explanation: Correct: large posts sit in more consequential countries and attract stronger officers, either of which would raise ratings without any staffing effect, so the recommendation works only if headcount is doing the work. Whether consumers rate accurately questions the measure but leaves the causal gap intact. Posts covering similar subjects would make the comparison cleaner without establishing that staffing drives quality. Whether reporting is a post's primary purpose bears on how much the improvement is worth, not on whether more officers would produce it.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the expert's inference?
choices: Border incidents rose slightly in the eleventh year
The primary armed group responsible for earlier incidents dissolved in 1999 for unrelated reasons
Other neighboring pairs have signed similar agreements
The agreement was never formally ratified by one of the parties
questions.explanation: Correct: an armed group dissolving in 1999 supplies a cause arriving almost exactly when the decline began, and it would produce the same 80 percent drop with no contribution from the agreement. Non-ratification by one party is weaker than it looks — an unratified agreement that still preceded the fall leaves the correlation entirely intact. A slight rise in the eleventh year is noise against a decade-long decline. Other pairs signing similar agreements says nothing about whether this one worked.

questions.stem: The department's argument overlooks the possibility that:
choices: Some officials may have opposed the reforms
The reforms may have reduced reporting of bribery rather than bribery itself
Bribery may have declined for reasons unrelated to the reforms
Thirty percent is a modest reduction
questions.explanation: Correct: the figure counts reports, not incidents, and reforms that intimidate complainants or dismantle reporting channels would produce exactly this 30 percent while bribery continued unchanged. That bribery fell for unrelated reasons is a real alternative but a weaker one, since it grants that the underlying conduct actually declined. Calling 30 percent modest disputes the size of the claimed success rather than its validity. Officials opposing the reforms describes the politics of adoption and says nothing about the measurement.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Rate increases below two points never cause appreciation
The currency will certainly appreciate within six months
The central bank raised rates in order to strengthen the currency
The currency has appreciated in every past instance meeting this condition, so appreciation is likely but not guaranteed
questions.explanation: Correct: an unbroken past record supports an expectation without guaranteeing the next case, since the stimulus reports what has happened rather than stating a law. Certainty overreads that record. Inferring that the bank raised rates in order to strengthen the currency imputes a motive the stimulus never gives; the relationship described is an observed regularity, not a stated intention. Concluding that smaller increases never cause appreciation infers from the absence of the stated condition that the outcome is absent, which the premise does not license.

questions.stem: The researcher's conclusion is most vulnerable because:
choices: Judicial independence is not the only determinant of investment
Her sample of countries is not specified
Per capita income may be a common cause of both judicial independence and investment
Foreign investment is difficult to measure consistently
questions.explanation: Correct: the researcher herself reports that per capita income tracks judicial independence, so income may drive both it and investment — a textbook confound she has documented and then ignored. An unspecified sample is a reporting gap that would not resolve the direction of causation even if filled. Inconsistent measurement of investment adds noise without explaining the association. Noting that judicial independence is not the only determinant is true but harmless, since a cause need not be the sole cause to be one.

questions.stem: The director's argument assumes that:
choices: Other organizations will cover the remaining countries
The three countries with greatest measured need can absorb concentrated resources effectively
Donors will approve the reallocation
Measured need is the same as actual need
questions.explanation: Correct: the premise that concentration yields more impact per dollar holds only where the resources can actually be used, and in a country with no delivery capacity additional funds accomplish nothing. Whether other organizations cover the remaining countries bears on the wider humanitarian picture, not on whether this agency's concentration works. Whether measured need matches actual need questions the choice of the three countries rather than the logic of concentrating. Donor approval is a practical hurdle, not a premise the reasoning depends on.

questions.stem: The critics' observation functions in the argument by:
choices: Proving that the officials misreported their figures
Demonstrating that the scanning equipment was defective
Showing that smuggling has shifted to other routes
Providing a control case suggesting the decline had a common external cause
questions.explanation: Correct: a comparable site without the intervention showing the same decline is precisely what a control provides — it isolates some shared external cause and leaves the equipment unsupported as an explanation. It does not show the equipment was defective; the equipment may work while the decline is attributable to something else. Nothing in the observation indicates smuggling moved to other routes, since attempts fell at both crossings. And nothing suggests the officials misreported: their figure may be accurate and still fail to prove their point.

questions.stem: The negotiator's inference is questionable because:
choices: Refusal to discuss an issue is at least as consistent with regarding it as too important to concede
The counterpart may lack authority to discuss the annex
The negotiator has misread the counterpart's tone
Fisheries agreements are usually negotiated separately
questions.explanation: Correct: silence supports opposite readings — a party may decline to discuss an issue because it does not matter, or because it matters so much that any discussion invites concession — so the refusal cannot establish indifference. Lacking authority is a genuine competing explanation but a narrower one, addressing why the counterpart could not engage rather than what the refusal reveals about priorities. That fisheries are usually negotiated separately is a procedural convention. Misreading tone concerns the negotiator's perception rather than the structure of his inference.

questions.stem: The economist's reasoning is most vulnerable to the criticism that:
choices: The comparison group is not specified
Growth rates are volatile from year to year
Some assistance is humanitarian rather than developmental
Assistance is typically directed toward countries already growing slowly
questions.explanation: Correct: assistance is allocated by need, so the poorest and slowest-growing countries receive the most, and that allocation rule alone produces the observed pattern with no effect of aid whatsoever. Volatile growth rates would add noise but not create a consistent yearly association. Some assistance being humanitarian refines what is being counted without touching the direction of causation. An unspecified comparison group is a reporting weakness that leaves the reverse-causation problem exactly where it was.

questions.stem: If the staff association's claim is accurate, the department's evidence is flawed because:
choices: Twenty-five percent is not a large improvement
The reduction reflects a change in what is measured rather than in service delivery
The staff association is a biased source
Processing time is not a good measure of service quality
questions.explanation: Correct: moving the slowest cases into an uncounted queue lowers the average without anything being processed faster, so the improvement is in the definition of the measure rather than in the service. Saying processing time poorly measures quality challenges the metric in principle, whereas the flaw here is that this metric was quietly redefined. Calling the staff association biased attacks the source rather than the claim. Disputing whether 25 percent is large concedes the figure and argues about its size.

questions.stem: The political scientist's argument is weakest in that it:
choices: Does not specify which organizations are meant
Relies on anecdotal evidence
Ignores the role of great powers in shaping resolutions
Assumes effectiveness requires compliance even when compliance is costly
questions.explanation: Correct: the argument counts an organization effective only if it can compel action against a member's interests, a standard almost no institution meets — and it makes invisible the functions such bodies actually perform, coordinating expectations, supplying information, and lowering the cost of agreement. Not naming the organizations makes the claim imprecise but would not rescue it once specified. The role of great powers in shaping resolutions explains why resolutions look as they do, not why ignoring them proves ineffectiveness. Calling the evidence anecdotal disputes its weight, whereas the defect is the standard being applied.

questions.stem: Which of the following can be concluded?
choices: Nothing can be concluded about Officer Chen's background from the information given
Officer Chen is not a senior officer
Officer Chen has served in the region previously
Officer Chen is a senior officer
questions.explanation: Correct: the premise says all region-experienced senior officers support the initiative, not that only they do, so Chen's support is compatible with any background whatsoever. Concluding Chen served in the region affirms the consequent — support is the stated effect, not a marker of the cause. Concluding Chen is a senior officer commits the same error on the other attribute. Concluding Chen is not a senior officer is equally unfounded, since nothing excludes the possibility either.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the evaluator's observation?
choices: The donor's two-year requirement systematically disadvantages institutional reform projects
Institutional reform projects are not worth funding
Projects should be evaluated after seven years
Measurable outcomes are a poor evaluation standard
questions.explanation: Correct: a rule demanding results within two years cannot be met by work whose results take five to seven, so such projects are filtered out by the timetable rather than by their merit. Concluding they are not worth funding draws the opposite lesson from the same facts and treats the donor's rule as a verdict on the work. Condemning measurable outcomes generally goes far beyond an observation about one interval. Prescribing seven-year evaluation proposes a remedy rather than stating what the observation shows.

questions.stem: The trade representative's argument assumes that:
choices: The agreement will be ratified
Imports will not increase at all
The affected sectors will find new employment quickly
Increased total exports outweigh any losses from increased imports
questions.explanation: Correct: 'benefit the country' is a claim about the net result, so it holds only if export gains exceed the losses in the import-exposed sectors the critics identify. Denying imports will rise at all overstates what the representative needs; he can concede the rise and still argue the balance is favorable. Displaced workers finding new jobs quickly would ease the harm but is not required for the net claim. Ratification is a procedural condition for the agreement taking effect, not a premise of the argument about its merits.

questions.stem: The training director's inference is questionable because:
choices: The officers who reach the highest proficiency may differ systematically in ability or ambition
Promotion rates vary by cone and grade
Language proficiency tests are imperfect measures
Not all posts require language proficiency
questions.explanation: Correct: reaching the highest proficiency is itself an achievement that selects for aptitude and persistence, and those same qualities drive promotion — so the gap may reflect who completes the training rather than any effect of the training. Imperfect proficiency tests add measurement noise without explaining the promotion difference. Variation by cone and grade is a reason to control the comparison, not a rival account of it. Some posts not requiring language says where the skill is used, not whether training caused advancement.

questions.stem: Which of the following must be true?
choices: The proposed convention is more likely to be enforced than convention without such a mechanism
The proposed convention satisfies a necessary condition for effective enforcement
Dispute-resolution mechanisms guarantee enforcement
The proposed convention will be effectively enforced
questions.explanation: Correct: the premise establishes the mechanism as necessary for effective enforcement, and the convention has it, so it has met that condition — no more follows. Concluding it will be enforced affirms the consequent, since necessary conditions do not guarantee outcomes. Calling it more likely to be enforced is a reasonable real-world judgment but not an entailment; necessary conditions carry no probabilistic weight. Saying such mechanisms guarantee enforcement inverts necessity into sufficiency, which the premise explicitly does not support.

questions.stem: The official's argument is most vulnerable to the criticism that it:
choices: Assumes preventive action is always available
Fails to define what counts as a crisis
Ignores the cost of maintaining the system
Treats a small number of past successes as guaranteeing future performance
questions.explanation: Correct: three cases are a thin base for a confident prediction, especially since crises the system missed entirely would never appear in its record of successes — the sample is selected on the outcome being claimed. An undefined threshold for 'crisis' makes the record harder to audit but does not create the inductive leap. Whether preventive action is available concerns what follows detection, a separate gap in the official's conclusion. The system's maintenance cost bears on whether to keep it, not on whether it will work.

questions.stem: The analyst's reasoning is flawed because it:
choices: Infers motive from consequence
Ignores the ambassador's conduct
Assumes the public was aware of the expulsion
Relies on approval ratings of uncertain accuracy
questions.explanation: Correct: an action producing a benefit does not show the benefit was its purpose; the expulsion may have been a genuine response to the ambassador's conduct with the rating rise an unanticipated by-product. Uncertainty in approval ratings questions the measurement rather than the leap from effect to intention. Public awareness of the expulsion is a precondition for any rating movement at all, which the stimulus already reports. Ignoring the ambassador's conduct gestures at the alternative explanation but describes an omission rather than naming the error.

questions.stem: The most serious problem with the report's conclusion is that:
choices: Performance ratings are subjective
The program may have been too short
Voluntary participation means participants may have been higher performers to begin with
Officers who declined may have had legitimate reasons
questions.explanation: Correct: when participation is optional, the officers who volunteer are plausibly the more motivated ones who would have rated well regardless, so the comparison measures who enrolled rather than what the training did. Subjective ratings introduce noise that affects both groups alike. A program being too short would explain a null result, not the positive one actually observed. Officers declining for legitimate reasons is fair to them but says nothing about whether the two groups were comparable to begin with.

questions.stem: The commentator's argument assumes that:
choices: Bilateral negotiations always succeed
Multilateral negotiations produce worse outcomes
All parties to a multilateral negotiation have distinct interests
Accommodating additional interests necessarily consumes additional time
questions.explanation: Correct: the argument moves from more interests to more time, which holds only if accommodating each additional interest actually consumes time rather than being absorbed in parallel. Bilateral negotiations always succeeding is far stronger than needed and concerns outcomes rather than duration. Multilateral talks producing worse outcomes is a claim about quality the commentator never makes. All parties having distinct interests is close but unnecessary: the argument survives if some parties share interests, provided accommodation still takes time.

questions.stem: The economist's response weakens the minister's argument by:
choices: Demonstrating that foreign suppliers are reliable
Denying that strategic vulnerability exists
Showing that domestic production is technically infeasible
Introducing a cost that must be weighed against the claimed security benefit
questions.explanation: Correct: the economist does not dispute the vulnerability; he prices the remedy, converting a one-sided security claim into a trade-off that now requires justification. He does not deny strategic vulnerability exists — his figure concedes the security premise and attaches a cost to acting on it. He shows domestic production is expensive, not technically infeasible; it demonstrably operates. And he says nothing about whether foreign suppliers are reliable, which is the very point the minister raised and the economist leaves standing.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best supported by the historical records described?
choices: The settlement's peace applied to relations among its participants rather than to their external conduct
European powers were more powerful than non-European societies
Wars outside Europe were caused by the settlement
The Vienna settlement eliminated warfare in the nineteenth century
questions.explanation: Correct: rare wars inside the club alongside frequent wars outside it supports a peace that was scoped to relations among the participants rather than general. Saying warfare was eliminated contradicts the second half of the record. That European powers were more capable than the societies they fought may well be true but is not what a distribution of wars between groups establishes. Attributing the external wars to the settlement asserts a causal link the records as described do not support.

questions.stem: The study's recommendation is most vulnerable to the objection that:
choices: Some officers request extensions
Officers who remain four years may be assigned to posts where such tours are offered for reasons that also affect reporting quality
Insight is difficult to measure
Longer tours are unpopular with officers
questions.explanation: Correct: four-year tours are not handed out at random — they cluster at particular posts and often go to officers with strong local knowledge or language ability, either of which would improve reporting independently of tour length. Difficulty measuring insight adds noise to the ratings without explaining the gap. Longer tours being unpopular bears on whether the recommendation can be implemented. Officers requesting extensions gestures at the selection problem but describes a mechanism rather than identifying why the comparison fails.

questions.stem: The ministry's argument depends on assuming that:
choices: The debt is denominated in domestic currency
A stable debt-to-GDP ratio indicates sustainability regardless of its level or the terms of the debt
GDP will continue to grow
Other countries maintain similar ratios
questions.explanation: Correct: stability says nothing about sustainability — the same 60 percent financed by short-dated foreign-currency borrowing at high interest is far more fragile than long-dated domestic debt, so the argument needs the level and terms to be irrelevant. Continued GDP growth and domestic-currency denomination are two of the specific factors that blanket assumption papers over, each necessary in its own way but narrower than the premise the argument requires. What other countries maintain is a comparison that establishes nothing about this country's position.

questions.stem: The observer's reasoning is flawed because:
choices: One party may be more credible than the other
Mutual accusation is evidence about what the parties claim, not about what they did
Ceasefire violations are difficult to verify
International monitors were not present
questions.explanation: Correct: both sides accusing each other is exactly what one expects whether blame is shared or entirely one-sided, since the guilty party has every incentive to accuse first — so symmetry of claims cannot establish symmetry of conduct. Difficulty verifying violations explains why the question is hard, not why this inference fails. One party being more credible is a reason to weigh the accusations unequally, which the observer has declined to do. Absent monitors describes a gap in evidence rather than the reasoning error.

questions.stem: The program officer's argument assumes that:
choices: Recipients who remain abroad provide no benefit to their home countries
The funds would produce more value in an alternative program
Seventy percent is an unusually high non-return rate compared with similar programs
Requiring recipients to return would raise the return rate
questions.explanation: Correct: the argument treats non-return as waste, which holds only if those who stay abroad deliver nothing homeward — an assumption that remittances, diaspora investment, and professional networks would defeat. Whether seventy percent is unusually high compares this program with others; the argument condemns it on its own terms and needs no benchmark. Cost relative to alternative uses would strengthen the case for cutting the program but is nowhere relied upon. Whether a return requirement would change behavior proposes a fix rather than exposing a premise.

questions.stem: Which of the following must be true?
choices: Country Z will join the customs union
Country Z has not joined the customs union
Country Z may or may not have joined the customs union
Country Z has joined the customs union
questions.explanation: Correct: joining is stated as sufficient for rising intra-regional trade, not necessary, so Z's increase is compatible with membership and with any number of other causes. Concluding Z joined affirms the consequent. Concluding Z did not join is equally unfounded, since membership would produce exactly this result. Predicting Z will join adds a forecast the premises give no basis for at all.

questions.stem: The official's proposal is most vulnerable to the criticism that it:
choices: Overlooks the cost of language training
Assumes language training is available for all languages
Moves from a claim about the strongest single predictor to a policy that ignores all other predictors
Assumes reporting is the only function of overseas posts
questions.explanation: Correct: being the strongest single predictor is compatible with explaining only a modest share of the outcome, so a rule using that variable alone discards everything the weaker predictors jointly contribute. Whether training exists for every language is an implementation constraint on staffing the policy. Training cost bears on affordability rather than on whether the rule selects well. Reporting not being a post's only function is a real limitation, but the statistical overreach is the error inside the reasoning itself.

questions.stem: The comparison described is unreliable because:
choices: The follow-up period was too short
Water quality was not measured directly
The two groups of villages differed systematically before the intervention
Health outcomes were self-reported
questions.explanation: Correct: villages chosen for their capacity to maintain infrastructure differ in wealth, governance, and baseline health, so the better outcomes may predate the project entirely — non-random assignment on a variable tied to the outcome is the definition of selection bias. Self-reported health adds measurement noise to both groups. A short follow-up would tend to understate any effect rather than manufacture one. Not measuring water quality directly leaves the mechanism unverified but does not explain why the two groups are incomparable.

questions.stem: The commentator's argument is weakest because it:
choices: Assumes that a policy which has not yet succeeded will not succeed
Fails to identify an alternative policy
Relies on an arbitrary time period
Ignores the humanitarian costs of sanctions
questions.explanation: Correct: a policy that has not produced results within a chosen interval may still produce them, particularly one that works by accumulating pressure — treating 'not yet' as 'not' is the whole of the error. Humanitarian costs are a serious argument for abandonment but a different one, which the commentator does not make. Failing to name an alternative is a gap in the recommendation rather than in the inference. Calling eighteen months arbitrary is closely related and correct as far as it goes, but the flaw would remain at any interval.

questions.stem: The department's use of the poll is problematic because:
choices: The sample size is not given
The question asked about a broad sentiment rather than the specific agreement
Sixty-two percent is not a supermajority
Polls are unreliable predictors of behavior
questions.explanation: Correct: almost everyone endorses 'expanding economic cooperation' in the abstract, while support for a particular agreement carrying particular concessions is a different and usually smaller number — the poll measures a sentiment and is being read as approval of a text. Whether 62 percent counts as a supermajority argues about the threshold rather than what was measured. An unreported sample size is an ordinary polling caveat. Polls predicting behavior poorly concerns what support implies, not whether this support was ever established.

questions.stem: The analyst's conclusion is most vulnerable to the objection that:
choices: Sixty years is a short period historically
Other disputes in the region have led to war
A record of no war may reflect deterrence or luck rather than the absence of risk
The states may have fought undeclared conflicts
questions.explanation: Correct: an absence of war is compatible with a dispute held in check by costly deterrence, which is a condition of high latent risk rather than low — and one that changes the moment the deterrent weakens. Sixty years being historically short is a related but weaker version of the same point. Other regional disputes leading to war concerns different cases. Undeclared conflicts would contradict the stimulus's own premise that the two have never fought.

questions.stem: The researcher's argument is most vulnerable to the criticism that:
choices: Peacekeeping missions vary widely in size and mandate
Some missions have lasted decades
Political violence is inconsistently defined across countries
Peacekeeping missions are deployed to countries already experiencing political violence
questions.explanation: Correct: missions go where violence already is, so the comparison sets the worst cases against the calmest ones and would show the same gap even if every mission halved the bloodshed it found. Inconsistent definitions of violence add measurement noise but would not systematically favor non-host countries. Variation in size and mandate is a reason to disaggregate the missions rather than a reason the comparison is invalid. Some missions lasting decades describes their duration, which is again a consequence of being sent to intractable places.

questions.stem: Which principle, if established, would most justify treating the export figures as evidence the program works?
choices: Programs should be given at least a year before evaluation
Export growth is always desirable
A change following an intervention may be attributed to it when comparable cases without the intervention show no similar change
Government programs should be evaluated by their measurable outputs
questions.explanation: Correct: it supplies exactly the missing link — a comparison group — converting a bare before-and-after figure into evidence about what the program caused. Evaluating programs by measurable outputs endorses using numbers without saying which numbers show causation, so the same 12 percent would count even if exports rose everywhere. Export growth always being desirable speaks to whether the goal is worth having. Giving programs a year before evaluation would postpone the judgment rather than justify the one already made.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, most supports the director's recommendation?
choices: Organizations should follow donor preferences in allocating resources
Humanitarian organizations should distribute resources equitably across all countries in need
An organization should allocate resources so as to maximize total impact, even at the cost of leaving some needs unaddressed
Need should be measured by objective indicators rather than by political salience
questions.explanation: Correct: the recommendation deliberately abandons some countries in order to raise the total, so it needs a principle that ranks aggregate impact above universal coverage and licenses the resulting omissions. Equitable distribution across all countries in need is the competing principle the director is rejecting. Following donor preferences would justify whatever donors happen to want, which may or may not be concentration. Preferring objective indicators of need defends how the three countries were picked, not the decision to concentrate at all.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the training director's conclusion?
choices: Officers assigned to the training by lottery were promoted at higher rates than those not assigned
The training program has been offered for over a decade
Officers report finding the training valuable
Language-designated positions are more numerous than they once were
questions.explanation: Correct: lottery assignment removes the self-selection that made the original comparison ambiguous, so a promotion gap that survives randomization is attributable to the training itself. A decade of operation establishes longevity, not effect. Officers finding the training valuable reports their satisfaction, which is not the outcome in dispute. More language-designated positions existing would help explain a promotion advantage through a route other than the training's own influence, which slightly undercuts rather than supports the claim.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the officer's conclusion?
choices: Documentation requirements are published on the embassy website
Some approved applicants brought no documentation at all
Applicants who brought extensive documentation were also more likely to own property and hold long-term employment
Interview length correlates with documentation volume
questions.explanation: Correct: property and steady employment are exactly what a consular officer weighs, so the paperwork is a symptom of the applicant's circumstances rather than a cause of approval — coaching a weak applicant to bring more would document weakness more thoroughly. Requirements being published means applicants could comply, which is compatible with the advice working. Some approved applicants bringing nothing shows the correlation is imperfect, not that it is spurious. Interview length tracking documentation volume is an unsurprising consequence with no bearing on refusals.

questions.stem: Which of the following is most strongly supported?
choices: The donor's portfolio will underrepresent institutional reform work relative to its share of identified need
Evaluators disagree with donors about project value
Institutional reform projects produce larger benefits than other projects
The donor should extend its requirement to seven years
questions.explanation: Correct: a two-year proof rule systematically excludes work that cannot produce evidence in two years, so reform projects drop out of the portfolio for reasons unrelated to how much reform is needed. Reform projects producing larger benefits is a claim about their value the evaluator never makes. Extending the requirement to seven years prescribes a fix rather than stating what follows. A general disagreement between evaluators and donors reads a dispute into what is presented as a single evaluator's observation about timing.

questions.stem: The economist's conclusion requires the assumption that:
choices: All assistance is delivered as direct budget support
Growth is measured consistently across countries
Assistance levels are not determined by the recipient's growth performance
Countries receiving assistance would otherwise receive private investment
questions.explanation: Correct: assistance is targeted at countries doing badly, so if allocation responds to growth the association is manufactured by the allocation rule and the arrow runs backwards. Assistance being delivered as budget support concerns its form, and the argument would face the same problem whatever the modality. Consistent growth measurement guards against noise rather than reversed causation. Recipients otherwise attracting private investment posits a further alternative to aid, which is a separate question from what the correlation shows.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the researcher's argument?
choices: Host governments sometimes object to mission deployments
Peacekeeping missions are expensive to maintain
Countries with missions and comparably violent countries without missions show identical trajectories of violence
Some missions have been withdrawn before their mandates expired
questions.explanation: Correct: matching hosts against comparably violent non-hosts removes the selection effect that is the obvious reply, and identical trajectories then mean the missions changed nothing. Missions being expensive bears on whether they are worth funding, not on whether they work. Early withdrawals describe how some missions ended. Host governments objecting to deployments reports political friction, which says nothing about the level of violence that followed.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most support the energy minister's position over the economist's?
choices: A state should accept economic costs to reduce dependence on suppliers it cannot control
Energy prices should be set by the market
Economic efficiency should govern all decisions about industrial policy
Domestic industries should be protected from foreign competition
questions.explanation: Correct: the economist has established a real cost, so the minister prevails only under a principle that accepts economic cost as the price of controlling supply — it converts the 40 percent premium from a refutation into an accepted expense. Making efficiency govern all industrial policy hands the argument to the economist. Protecting domestic industry from competition is a broader protectionist claim resting on producer interest rather than the security ground the minister actually offers. Letting the market set prices again favors the economist's side.

questions.stem: The official's argument assumes that:
choices: The next crisis will resemble the previous three in ways relevant to detection
The early-warning system is operated by trained analysts
No crises have been missed by the system
Preventive action always succeeds when taken
questions.explanation: Correct: three past successes support a prediction only if the next case is detectable by the same signals; a crisis of a different type would slip past a system tuned to the previous three. Trained analysts operating the system concerns how it runs rather than what it can see. Preventive action always succeeding goes to what happens after detection, which the conclusion mentions but does not depend on. No crises having been missed would strengthen the record, yet the argument as stated rests only on the three it claims.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most undermines the historian's explanation?
choices: Some peacetime alliances have dissolved quickly
Time pressure affects all negotiations to some degree
Wartime alliances often involve more parties
Peacetime alliances are typically formed between states with pre-existing alignment of interests
questions.explanation: Correct: if peacetime alliances form between states already aligned, the shared interests explain both the calm negotiation and the long life, so the historian's causal story is displaced by a common cause. Wartime alliances involving more parties offers a rival mechanism only if size shortens alliances, which is not established. Time pressure affecting all negotiations concedes a difference of degree and leaves the explanation standing. Some peacetime alliances dissolving quickly notes exceptions to a stated tendency.

questions.stem: If both the department's figure and the staff association's claim are accurate, which is best supported?
choices: Average processing time for the cases still counted has fallen, while overall performance is unknown
Complex cases now take longer than before
Service quality has declined
The department has deliberately misled the public
questions.explanation: Correct: both claims can be true at once — the counted cases really are faster, while the complex cases sit outside the average, so the overall picture is simply unmeasured. Saying the department deliberately misled infers intent from a definitional change. Saying complex cases now take longer is unsupported; being uncounted is not the same as being slower. Saying service quality has declined asserts the opposite of the department's claim with no more evidence than the department had.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the section chief's conclusion?
choices: A major bilateral dispute over fishing rights dominated local coverage during the same period
The embassy's social media following grew during the year
Other embassies in the country also increased social media output
Local journalists rarely use social media professionally
questions.explanation: Correct: a bilateral dispute dominating coverage supplies an independent cause of the decline in favorable mentions, breaking the link the chief drew from mere co-occurrence. A growing social media following measures reach rather than journalists' reaction. Other embassies also increasing output would help only if their coverage held steady, which is not stated. Journalists rarely using social media professionally is closer to helpful, but it undercuts the mechanism weakly, since coverage can be shaped by material journalists never see directly.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most justify abandoning the sanctions regime?
choices: Sanctions should never be imposed on countries with which trade is substantial
A policy that has not achieved its objective within eighteen months will not achieve it
Policies should be reviewed periodically
A policy should be abandoned once its costs to the imposing states exceed the value of the change it seeks
questions.explanation: Correct: the commentator infers from eighteen months of failure to permanent failure, so only a principle that treats that interval as decisive will carry the argument — it is a strong principle, but it is the one the reasoning needs. A cost-exceeds-benefit test would justify abandonment on grounds the commentator never invokes, since no costs are mentioned. Never sanctioning substantial trading partners turns on a fact not in evidence. Periodic review licenses reconsideration rather than abandonment.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best supported by the information given?
choices: Smuggling has increased overall in the region
The scanning equipment had no effect on smuggling
The nearby crossing also received new equipment
The decline in smuggling attempts at the first crossing is not clearly attributable to the equipment
questions.explanation: Correct: a comparable crossing without new equipment falling by the same amount points to a shared external cause, leaving the equipment unsupported as the explanation without being refuted. Concluding the equipment had no effect overstates this: a real effect could be masked or could coexist with the regional cause. An overall increase in smuggling contradicts the reported declines. Concluding the nearby crossing also received equipment denies the premise on which the critics' point rests.

questions.stem: The department's argument assumes that:
choices: The poll used a representative sample
Respondents understood the question
Public support is necessary for ratification
Support for 'expanding economic cooperation' translates into support for this specific agreement
questions.explanation: Correct: the poll asked about a general aspiration, and the department reports it as backing for a particular text with particular concessions — the inference lives or dies on those two things being the same. A representative sample and respondents understanding the question are generic polling conditions the department would need for any reading of the number. Public support being necessary for ratification concerns what follows if support exists, not whether this poll established it.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most support the study's recommendation?
choices: When a measured difference in output tracks a difference in assignment length, assignment length should be adjusted to favor the better-performing arrangement
Personnel policy should be set by the preferences of the officers affected
Officers should be assigned to posts where their language skills are strongest
Reporting quality should be the primary criterion for evaluating overseas posts
questions.explanation: Correct: the recommendation converts an observed association into a policy change, so it needs a principle licensing exactly that move from measured difference to adjusted rule. Setting policy by officers' preferences appeals to a consideration the study never raises. Assigning officers by language strength proposes a different criterion altogether. Making reporting quality the primary criterion for evaluating posts elevates the outcome measure without connecting it to tour length, so the recommendation still does not follow.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most support the political scientist's conclusion?
choices: Resolutions that are routinely ignored should not be adopted
An institution is effective only if it can secure compliance that members would not otherwise offer
International organizations should be funded in proportion to their results
States are the primary actors in international politics
questions.explanation: Correct: the evidence is that states ignore resolutions when compliance is costly, which condemns the institutions only under a standard that equates effectiveness with compelling unwanted compliance. Funding organizations in proportion to results is a budgeting rule that presupposes an effectiveness measure rather than supplying one. States being the primary actors is a background claim about international politics. Saying ignored resolutions should not be adopted advises a change in practice and leaves the effectiveness question untouched.

questions.stem: Which of the following must be true?
choices: State F has not accepted the optional protocol
Some states that accepted the protocol do not permit complaints
State F will accept the protocol in future
State F has violated the protocol
questions.explanation: Correct: acceptance guarantees individual complaints, and F does not permit them, so F cannot be among the accepting states — denying the consequent, which is valid. Predicting future acceptance forecasts beyond anything the premises contain. Saying F has violated the protocol presumes F is bound by it, when the inference establishes the opposite. Saying some accepting states do not permit complaints contradicts the premise that all of them do.

questions.stem: Which of the following can be properly concluded?
choices: Addressing a priority sector is necessary but not sufficient for funding
No projects in priority sectors are funded
The department's criteria are inconsistently applied
Addressing a priority sector guarantees funding
questions.explanation: Correct: 'only if' makes priority-sector status a requirement, and the second premise supplies projects that met it and were still refused, which shows it does not by itself secure funding. Saying it guarantees funding is exactly what the second premise refutes. Saying no priority-sector projects are funded misreads 'some are not' as 'none are'. Calling the criteria inconsistent assumes sector is the only criterion, when unfunded projects may simply have failed some other requirement.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best supported?
choices: Completing a hardship tour guarantees promotion
Promotion requires nothing beyond a hardship tour
Completing a hardship tour is necessary but not sufficient for promotion
Most officers who complete hardship tours are promoted
questions.explanation: Correct: every promoted officer had a hardship tour, which makes it a requirement, and some who completed one went unpromoted, which shows it is not enough — the two premises pin down exactly this. Saying it guarantees promotion is refuted by the second premise. Saying most who complete one are promoted quantifies a proportion neither premise supplies. Saying promotion requires nothing beyond a hardship tour contradicts the existence of officers who completed one and were passed over.

questions.stem: Which of the following follows?
choices: The fisheries agreement was poorly drafted
The fisheries agreement will not survive a change of government
No agreement survives a change of government
The fisheries agreement has already collapsed
questions.explanation: Correct: the generalization covers every agreement reached under time pressure without exception, and the fisheries agreement is stated to be one, so it falls under the rule. Saying it has already collapsed is premature, since the rule speaks to what happens at a change of government, which may not have occurred. Saying no agreement survives a change of government drops the time-pressure qualifier and overgeneralizes. Calling it poorly drafted supplies an explanation the premises never offer.

questions.stem: Which of the following must be true?
choices: New instructions were sent but not received
The delegation received new instructions
The delegation will table a revised text later
The delegation did not receive new instructions
questions.explanation: Correct: new instructions would produce a revised text, and none has been tabled, so the instructions cannot have arrived — a valid denial of the consequent. Concluding the delegation did receive instructions contradicts that. Saying it will table a text later speculates about the future from a premise about the present. Saying instructions were sent but not received invents a delivery failure; the premises concern receipt only, and any story about transmission is added from outside.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best supported?
choices: The reform causes inflation to fall
Inflation in Country K probably fell, though it may not have
Inflation in Country K has certainly fallen
Inflation in Country K has not fallen
questions.explanation: Correct: 'most' supports an expectation rather than a certainty, and three years is past the two-year window, so the likely case is that inflation fell while K may sit among the minority. Saying it has certainly fallen converts a majority into a guarantee. Saying it has not fallen backs the less likely branch with no reason given. Saying the reform causes inflation to fall states a general causal claim, whereas the premise reports only what most adopters observed.

questions.stem: Which of the following can be concluded about the new system?
choices: It is effective
It will detect the next crisis
It satisfies a condition that all effective systems satisfy
It is more effective than systems lacking political analysis
questions.explanation: Correct: the report makes the combination a feature of all effective systems, so possessing it places the new system in the company of effective ones without settling whether it is one — necessary conditions work in that direction only. Concluding it is effective affirms the consequent. Calling it more effective than systems lacking political analysis compares performance the premise never ranks. Saying it will detect the next crisis predicts an outcome that even genuine effectiveness would not guarantee.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best supported?
choices: The literacy program did not actually meet its targets
The donor has discontinued all funding
Meeting targets is necessary for renewal but does not guarantee it
The donor violated its own policy
questions.explanation: Correct: 'only for' makes meeting targets a requirement, and here a program met them and was still not renewed, which shows the requirement is not the whole of the decision. Saying the donor violated its own policy misreads the rule, which forbids renewing programs that miss targets and never obliges renewal of those that meet them. Saying the program did not actually meet its targets denies a stated premise. Saying the donor has discontinued all funding generalizes from one case.

questions.stem: Which of the following must be true?
choices: The Senate has rejected few treaties
Bipartisan sponsorship guarantees ratification
The pending treaty differs from every treaty rejected in the past fifty years in at least one respect
The pending treaty will be ratified
questions.explanation: Correct: every rejected treaty lacked bipartisan sponsorship and this one has it, so it differs from each of them in at least that respect — a modest conclusion, and exactly what the premises deliver. Saying it will be ratified treats the absence of a feature common to failures as a guarantee of success. Saying bipartisan sponsorship guarantees ratification states that guarantee outright. Saying the Senate has rejected few treaties quantifies a record the premises leave open.

questions.stem: Which of the following can be properly inferred?
choices: All members of the working group have doctoral degrees
All economists are members of the working group
No members of the working group have doctoral degrees
Some members of the working group may have doctoral degrees, but this does not follow necessarily
questions.explanation: Correct: the doctoral premise is restricted to economists in the department, and nothing places the working group's economists there, so they may or may not hold doctorates. Saying all members have doctorates ignores both the restriction and the members who are not economists at all. Saying none do rules out a possibility the premises leave open. Saying all economists belong to the working group reverses 'some members are economists' into a claim about every economist.

questions.stem: The section's argument assumes that:
choices: The conditions that motivated the previous boycotts still obtain
The opposition is united
Boycotts are an effective strategy
The election will be held on schedule
questions.explanation: Correct: past behavior predicts future behavior only if the situation that produced it persists; a new electoral commission or a credible guarantee could end the boycott whatever strategy was last announced. Opposition unity would matter to whether a boycott could be maintained, which is a further question. The election being held on schedule concerns timing rather than the opposition's choice. Boycotts being effective goes to whether the strategy is wise, and parties persist with unwise strategies.

questions.stem: The analyst's reasoning is most vulnerable to the criticism that it:
choices: Relies on too few years of data
Ignores imports entirely
Assumes GDP is measured accurately
Treats co-movement as evidence that one variable drives the other
questions.explanation: Correct: exports and GDP rising together is what one expects whether exports drive output or a domestic boom lifts both, and exports are a component of GDP besides — so the movement cannot establish the direction. Relying on too few years disputes the sample, and the same problem would survive a century of data. Ignoring imports concerns the trade balance rather than the causal claim. Assuming accurate GDP measurement questions the data instead of the inference drawn from it.

questions.stem: The official's argument depends on the assumption that:
choices: Officers selected for the accelerated program are comparable to those in the standard program
All officers require the same proficiency level
Language training is the department's largest expense
The proficiency test is administered annually
questions.explanation: Correct: the two programs are compared as if only their length differed, but if the accelerated course takes the quickest learners, equal outcomes mean the shortcut worked for them and would not survive being applied to everyone. Language training being the largest expense is the motive for shortening it. All officers needing the same proficiency concerns the standard rather than the comparison. The test being annual is a scheduling detail with no bearing on who was enrolled where.

questions.stem: The researcher's argument is weakest in that it:
choices: Overlooks regional courts
Adopts a standard of legitimacy that few institutions of any kind could satisfy
Assumes states are unitary actors
Does not identify which courts are meant
questions.explanation: Correct: the standard demands compliance precisely when compliance is inconvenient, which almost no institution — domestic courts included — reliably achieves, so it would strip legitimacy from nearly everything and thereby loses its force as a test. Not identifying the courts makes the claim imprecise but does not rescue it once specified. Assuming states are unitary actors simplifies who complies. Overlooking regional courts asks for more cases rather than questioning the criterion being applied.

questions.stem: The security adviser's reasoning is flawed because:
choices: Prohibited items are rare in any case
The previous procedure also detected nothing
The absence of detections is equally consistent with the procedure failing to detect anything
The procedure may be expensive
questions.explanation: Correct: a screen that catches everything and a screen that catches nothing produce the same empty log, so zero detections cannot distinguish success from failure without some independent check. The procedure being expensive concerns its cost. Prohibited items being rare is closer, since it offers a third reading of the same silence, but it grants that the count means something and merely explains it. The previous procedure detecting nothing supplies a comparison that leaves both records equally uninformative.

questions.stem: The delegation's argument is most vulnerable because it:
choices: Does not specify the substance of the proposal
Overlooks the possibility of a fourth party
Treats a position's location between two others as establishing that it is reasonable
Assumes the other parties negotiated in good faith
questions.explanation: Correct: a midpoint is defined by whatever the other two positions happen to be, so an extreme pair makes an extreme proposal look moderate — position between others is a fact about arithmetic rather than about merit. Assuming good faith concerns the others' conduct. Not specifying the substance is a gap in the presentation, though the flaw would remain with the substance fully spelled out. Overlooking a fourth party would change where the midpoint falls without repairing the reasoning that midpoints are reasonable.

questions.stem: The economist's conclusion is most vulnerable to the objection that:
choices: Employment might have grown absent the increase, so flat employment could conceal a loss
Employment is difficult to measure
One year is too short a period
The minimum wage affects only some workers
questions.explanation: Correct: the comparison that matters is against what employment would have been, not against what it was, so a sector on a rising trend that then held flat has lost jobs invisibly. One year being too short concerns the window rather than the missing counterfactual. The minimum wage affecting only some workers narrows the population at risk. Employment being difficult to measure adds noise to the figure without explaining why an unchanged figure fails to prove the point.

questions.stem: The commentator's argument is weakest in that it:
choices: Treats one qualification as though it were the only relevant one
Attacks the ambassador personally
Assumes regional experience can be measured
Ignores the confirmation process
questions.explanation: Correct: an ambassador's fitness rests on several things — negotiating skill, standing at home, management, access to the leadership — so lacking one of them cannot settle the question. Saying the commentator attacks her personally misdescribes an argument that cites a professional qualification rather than her character. Assuming regional experience can be measured questions how the premise was established. Ignoring the confirmation process points to who decides rather than to the leap from one gap to unfitness.

questions.stem: The official's argument overlooks the possibility that:
choices: The policy may be expensive
The proposed policy also has serious drawbacks
Some alternatives were not considered
The drawbacks could be mitigated
questions.explanation: Correct: showing that every alternative is flawed leaves open that the proposal is flawed too, perhaps worse — the argument establishes that the options are all imperfect and then treats one of them as vindicated. Saying some alternatives were not considered questions how complete the survey was, and the flaw survives a complete one. Saying the drawbacks could be mitigated applies to the proposal and the alternatives alike. Cost is one possible drawback rather than the gap in the reasoning.

questions.stem: The study's recommendation assumes that:
choices: Budget size drives coverage rather than both reflecting the importance of the relationship
Favorable coverage benefits the sending state
Media coverage is accurately measured
All embassies pursue the same objectives
questions.explanation: Correct: important relationships attract both bigger budgets and closer, warmer coverage, so the recommendation works only if the money is doing the work rather than both tracking the same underlying priority. Accurate measurement of coverage guards against noise in the outcome. All embassies pursuing the same objectives would make the comparison cleaner without establishing causation. Favorable coverage benefiting the sending state matters to whether the goal is worth pursuing, not to whether budgets achieve it.

questions.stem: The negotiator's inference is questionable because:
choices: The other delegation may lack instructions
Negotiations often involve posturing
Domestic pressure is difficult to observe
Hardening without explanation is consistent with several motives, including tactical ones
questions.explanation: Correct: a delegation may harden without explanation because it is squeezed at home, because it is manufacturing leverage, because it is waiting out the clock, or because it has been told to hold — so the behavior underdetermines the cause. Domestic pressure being hard to observe explains why the negotiator resorted to inference. The delegation lacking instructions names one of those competing motives rather than the flaw. Negotiations involving posturing gestures at another, again supplying an instance rather than the diagnosis.

questions.stem: The department's evidence is weak primarily because:
choices: The system was expensive to install
Officers may dislike the new system
Administrative tasks are hard to define
Self-reported time estimates may not reflect actual time spent
questions.explanation: Correct: officers are estimating their own hours after a change they know is meant to save time, and such estimates drift toward the expected answer, so the reported drop may not correspond to any real one. Officers disliking the system would bias reports in the opposite direction and so cannot explain a favorable result. Administrative tasks being hard to define makes the boundary fuzzy for everyone alike. Installation cost bears on whether the savings are worth it, which presupposes the savings are real.

questions.stem: The bureau's argument is most vulnerable to the objection that:
choices: Cable counts are recorded inconsistently
The post may be newly opened
Other posts may produce excessive cables
Cable volume may not measure the value of a post's work
questions.explanation: Correct: a post may write few cables and still run a consular section, manage an assistance portfolio, or hold access no one else has, so counting cables measures output on one dimension and treats it as the whole. Other posts producing excessive cables would deflate this post's ranking, which is a version of the same point but rests on an unsupported charge against them. Inconsistent recording questions the accuracy of the count. The post being newly opened offers an excuse for a low count rather than challenging the measure.

questions.stem: The adviser's reasoning is most vulnerable because:
choices: Exchange rates are volatile
Past crises sharing a precursor does not establish that the next will share it
Currency data may be unreliable
Three cases is a small sample
questions.explanation: Correct: the next crisis may originate in a border incident, a succession, or a commodity shock, and a monitor tuned to exchange rates would watch it develop unseen — a shared precursor in past cases is not a rule for future ones. Exchange rates being volatile describes the indicator's behavior. Unreliable currency data questions the input. A small sample is closely related and correct as far as it goes, but the leap would remain unjustified even with thirty past crises, since the argument still assumes the next resembles them.

questions.stem: The commentator's argument is flawed because:
choices: The agreement may be ambiguous
Historic agreements often fail
Only one signatory's view is reported
Public characterization of an agreement is not evidence of intent to implement it
questions.explanation: Correct: parties call agreements historic for domestic audiences, for the other side, and to lock in credit, so the description is a public posture rather than evidence about what either intends to do. Saying historic agreements often fail asserts a general track record the commentator could dispute. Saying only one signatory's view is reported contradicts the stimulus, which reports both. Saying the agreement may be ambiguous names a separate reason it might fail rather than identifying what is wrong with the inference.

questions.stem: The officer's argument assumes that:
choices: The source has no motive to deceive
The source has access to privileged information
The information can be independently verified
Past accuracy predicts current accuracy for this source
questions.explanation: Correct: the inference runs from one past success to present reliability, which holds only if accuracy carries forward — sources are cultivated, turned, or moved away from access. Having no motive to deceive would be a further reason to trust the source, and the officer argues from the record instead. Independent verification is what one does rather than relying on reliability. Access to privileged information concerns whether the source is positioned to know, which is a different qualification from whether past accuracy predicts future accuracy.

questions.stem: The department's evidence is weakest because:
choices: Surveys of alumni are expensive
Not all alumni respond to surveys
A decade is too short to assess goodwill
Alumni who accepted scholarships may have held favorable views beforehand
questions.explanation: Correct: applicants who seek and accept a scholarship from a sponsoring country are already inclined toward it, so favorable views a decade later may be the disposition that produced the application rather than anything the program built. A decade being too short works against the objection, since goodwill that persists that long is the harder test. Surveys being expensive concerns the cost of evidence. Incomplete response is a real limitation, but it adds uncertainty rather than explaining the result.

questions.stem: The policy paper's argument is most vulnerable because it:
choices: Ignores the views of other parties
Overstates the number of statutes affected
Assumes amendments would be controversial
Identifies a cost of joining without weighing it against any benefit
questions.explanation: Correct: twelve amendments are a price, and a price settles nothing until it is set against what joining would deliver — the paper reaches a conclusion with only one side of the ledger in view. Overstating the number of statutes disputes the figure, and the argument would be equally one-sided if the figure were exact. Assuming the amendments would be controversial reads difficulty into the count. Ignoring other parties' views brings in outside opinion rather than the missing benefit.

questions.stem: The analyst's conclusion is most vulnerable to the objection that:
choices: International observation is politically contested
Observers visited only a subset of stations, which may not have been representative
Irregularities may occur after polls close
Observers may lack local language skills
questions.explanation: Correct: observers cannot be everywhere, and stations they can reach are typically the accessible, urban, better-run ones, so a clean report from that subset does not extend to the stations no one saw. Language skills bear on what observers could understand at the stations they visited. Irregularities after polls close identifies one particular gap in coverage, narrower than the sampling problem itself. International observation being politically contested concerns how the report will be received rather than what it can show.

questions.stem: The official's argument assumes that:
choices: Applicants can afford a higher fee
Demand will not fall if fees rise
Fees should track the cost of providing the service
Other posts charge more
questions.explanation: Correct: the argument treats an unchanged fee against rising costs as itself a reason to raise it, which follows only if fees are supposed to recover cost — a fee set to keep travel accessible, or capped by statute, would not be indicted by the same facts. Whether applicants can afford it and whether demand would fall are consequences of raising the fee rather than premises of the case for raising it. What other posts charge is a comparison the official never draws.

questions.stem: The commentator's argument is weakest in that it:
choices: Does not define coherence
Ignores the role of allies
Assumes the two situations are alike in the respects that matter
Relies on only two examples
questions.explanation: Correct: different positions are inconsistent only if the cases are relevantly similar, and the two regions may differ in whether a population was annexed, whether a referendum occurred, or what the parties themselves have agreed — so the charge presupposes an equivalence it never argues.
