Relying on two examples questions the sample when one genuine contradiction would suffice. Not defining coherence makes the standard vague. Ignoring allies brings in outside influence rather than the assumed likeness.

questions.stem: The economist's argument assumes that:
choices: The basket includes only manufactured goods
The two countries have similar income levels
Exchange rates are set by governments
The goods in the basket are genuinely comparable and freely tradable between the two countries
questions.explanation: Correct: a price gap indicates overvaluation only if the same goods could in principle move between the markets; if the basket includes haircuts, rents, or anything else insulated by transport costs or barriers, the gap reflects non-tradables rather than the exchange rate. Similar income levels would make the comparison more natural without being required. Governments setting exchange rates concerns the regime rather than the measurement. A basket of only manufactured goods would help the argument rather than being assumed by it.

questions.stem: The evaluation's conclusion is flawed because:
choices: Negotiating ability varies by context
Graduates may have forgotten the training
Confidence and ability are distinct, and training can raise one without the other
The survey sample was small
questions.explanation: Correct: training reliably raises confidence, sometimes fastest in those who learned least, so a self-rating cannot stand in for the capability the evaluation claims to have improved. A small sample adds uncertainty to a measure that would be the wrong measure at any size. Graduates forgetting the training would depress the reports rather than inflate them. Negotiating ability varying by context complicates how one would assess it, which is a difficulty for the fix rather than the flaw in the finding.

questions.stem: The specialist's argument assumes that:
choices: War is always economically ruinous
Both governments will act on a calculation of economic interest
Neither government faces domestic opposition
The two economies are equally dependent on trade
questions.explanation: Correct: the prediction runs from ruinous consequences to restraint, and that step needs the governments to be weighing economic interest — leaders facing a nationalist surge, a succession crisis, or a perceived existential threat have gone to war knowing the cost. Equal trade dependence would matter to how the costs fall. War always being ruinous is a stronger general claim than this case needs. Neither government facing domestic opposition is not required and, if anything, cuts against the prediction.

questions.stem: The official's argument commits which error?
choices: Treating already-spent resources as a reason to continue
Confusing correlation with causation
Appealing to popular opinion
Assuming the program has no benefits
questions.explanation: Correct: money already spent is gone whether the program continues or stops, so it cannot bear on which course is better from here — only the remaining costs and benefits can. Assuming the program has no benefits describes an argument the official is not making; he simply never reaches them. Confusing correlation with causation names a different error entirely. Appealing to popular opinion would rest the case on what people think, and the official rests it on what has been spent.

questions.stem: The researcher's conclusion is most vulnerable because:
choices: Government effectiveness is hard to measure
Effective governments may permit press freedom rather than the reverse
Press freedom rankings are subjective
The sample excludes some countries
questions.explanation: Correct: capable, confident governments are the ones that tolerate scrutiny, so effectiveness may produce press freedom and the association would look identical — the direction is exactly what the argument needs and never establishes. Subjective rankings and hard-to-measure effectiveness both question the quality of the two measures rather than the link between them. An incomplete sample raises coverage, which would matter if the concern were generalization rather than which variable moves the other.

questions.stem: The information about application volume weakens the department's claim by suggesting that:
choices: The fraud decline may reflect fewer applications rather than deterrence
The interview requirement was unpopular
Fraudulent applications are hard to detect
Interviews are expensive to conduct
questions.explanation: Correct: halving the applications halves the pool from which fraud can come, so the count could fall by the same proportion with the fraud rate untouched — the department's figure needs to be expressed per application before it shows anything. The requirement being unpopular concerns applicants' reaction. Fraud being hard to detect suggests the count understates the problem in both periods alike. Interviews being expensive bears on whether the measure is worth its cost rather than on whether it deterred anyone.

questions.stem: The adviser's argument assumes that:
choices: The efficiency difference stems from management practices rather than differing objectives and constraints
Performance management is inexpensive to implement
Government agencies resist reform
Private firms measure efficiency accurately
questions.explanation: Correct: firms pursue profit under competition while agencies pursue mandates under statute, oversight, and public accountability, so the efficiency gap may be produced by those conditions and the practices would not transfer with the results. Whether firms measure efficiency accurately questions the premise's basis. Agencies resisting reform predicts a difficulty in adoption. Performance management being inexpensive concerns the cost of the change rather than whether it explains the difference the adviser is relying on.

questions.stem: The commentator's argument overlooks that a treaty may:
choices: Be cheaper than domestic legislation
Attract additional signatories
Require periodic review
Lock in current compliance against future change
questions.explanation: Correct: present compliance is voluntary and revocable, and a treaty converts it into an obligation that survives a change of government or of circumstances — which is precisely the work the commentator says is unnecessary. Being cheaper than domestic legislation compares two routes to the same standard. Attracting additional signatories concerns states outside the current group rather than the parties in question. Requiring periodic review is a procedural feature and, if anything, a cost of joining.

questions.stem: The analyst's conclusion is most vulnerable to the objection that:
choices: Five years is an arbitrary threshold
The region may be unrepresentative
Power-sharing provisions may be adopted precisely in the most intractable conflicts
Some agreements without power-sharing also collapsed
questions.explanation: Correct: negotiators reach for power-sharing when a conflict is deeply divided and no side can win outright, so the provision marks the hardest cases and the collapses may be the conflict's doing rather than the clause's. Calling five years arbitrary disputes the threshold. Some non-power-sharing agreements also collapsing would weaken the association, though it concedes the comparison's logic. The region being unrepresentative limits how far the finding generalizes rather than explaining it within the region.

questions.stem: The department's evidence is weak because:
choices: The assessment may be too easy
Participants may have discussed the answers
Knowing the right answer on an assessment differs from behaving accordingly
Training is expensive
questions.explanation: Correct: an ethics assessment measures whether participants can identify the correct answer, and the behavior at issue occurs under pressure, in private, with something to gain — so a score can rise while conduct does not. The assessment being too easy questions its difficulty rather than what it captures. Participants discussing answers describes a way the scores could be inflated, a narrower problem. Training being expensive concerns cost-effectiveness, which presupposes the effect is real.

questions.stem: The officer's reasoning is flawed because:
choices: The allegation may itself be unfounded
The host government may be telling the truth
Denials are sometimes accompanied by evidence
That denials are routine does not establish that this denial is false
questions.explanation: Correct: guilty and innocent governments both deny, so the routineness of denials leaves this one exactly where it started — the officer needs evidence about this case rather than a base rate. Saying the host government may be telling the truth restates the possibility the flaw allows rather than naming the flaw. Denials sometimes coming with evidence describes a stronger kind of denial than this one. The allegation itself being unfounded concerns the other side of the dispute and is not what the officer's inference gets wrong.

questions.stem: The specialist's argument assumes that:
choices: Relief can be reversed if compliance lapses
The five conditions were not intended to be satisfied jointly before relief
The remaining two conditions are unimportant
The target government acted in good faith
questions.explanation: Correct: conditions attached to sanctions relief are normally cumulative, and if these five are, then meeting three is partial compliance rather than grounds for relief — the argument only works by reading the list as a menu. Saying the remaining two are unimportant is stronger than the argument needs and would have to be argued separately. Good faith concerns the target's motives rather than the structure of the conditions. Reversibility of relief is a safeguard that matters after the decision, not a premise of it.

questions.stem: The projection is most vulnerable to the objection that:
choices: Forty percent is an unusually large improvement
Digitization is expensive
Processing time is hard to measure
The pilot population is unrepresentative of applicants elsewhere
questions.explanation: Correct: a pilot run among highly connected urban applicants tests digitisation under the most favorable conditions available, and applicants with poor connectivity or limited digital literacy will not reproduce the gain, so the 40 percent does not travel. Digitisation being expensive concerns cost rather than effect. Processing time being hard to measure questions the pilot's number. Forty percent being unusually large expresses suspicion of the result without identifying why it fails to generalize.

questions.stem: The analyst's reasoning is most vulnerable because:
choices: Eighteen months is a short average
The parliamentary system may have changed
Coalitions sometimes reform after collapsing
An average tells you little about when any particular coalition will end
questions.explanation: Correct: an average is compatible with wide dispersion, so a coalition at twenty months may be perfectly ordinary — some run three months, others four years, and the mean predicts none of them individually. Calling eighteen months a short average comments on the figure rather than on the inference drawn from it. The system possibly having changed questions whether the historical base still applies, a narrower objection. Coalitions reforming after collapsing concerns what happens next rather than whether this one is about to end.

questions.stem: The commentator's argument is flawed because:
choices: Summits have multiple purposes
Parties sometimes deliberately avoid a communiqué while still achieving their aims
Communiqués are often drafted in advance
Failure is difficult to define
questions.explanation: Correct: parties skip a communiqué to avoid publicising concessions, to leave language unsettled, or because a quiet understanding served them better — so the absence of a document is not the absence of a result. Communiqués often being drafted in advance is true and would if anything make one easier to issue. Summits having multiple purposes is closely related but stops at noting breadth. Failure being hard to define concerns the standard rather than the leap from no document to no achievement.

questions.stem: The official's argument is weakest in that it:
choices: Ignores the views of experts
Assumes the public is well informed
Overstates the size of the majority
Treats popularity as establishing that a policy is justified
questions.explanation: Correct: what a majority wants and what is defensible are different questions, and majorities have supported policies that were unjust or self-defeating — the argument supplies no reason beyond the count. Overstating the majority disputes the number, and the reasoning would be equally weak with an accurate one. Ignoring experts proposes a rival authority rather than identifying why popularity is the wrong ground. Assuming the public is well informed is close, yet the argument would still fail even among perfectly informed voters.

questions.stem: The researcher's conclusion is most vulnerable to the objection that:
choices: Distance can be measured in several ways
Income is difficult to measure in rural areas
The road may have been routed through areas that were already better off
The road may be recently built
questions.explanation: Correct: roads are routed to serve places that already have commerce and population, so proximity may mark prior prosperity and the income gap could predate the construction entirely. Income being hard to measure in rural areas adds noise to both groups. The road being recently built would leave too little time for an effect, which argues against a real effect rather than explaining the observed gap. Distance being measurable in several ways concerns the precision of the comparison rather than what drives it.

questions.stem: The department's inference is questionable because:
choices: Officers may be unaware of the standard
An absence of discipline may reflect weak enforcement rather than good compliance
The standard may be new
Discipline records may be confidential
questions.explanation: Correct: a standard nobody enforces and a standard everybody keeps produce identical records, so a clean slate cannot distinguish them without some evidence about how vigorously conduct is examined. The standard being new limits how much record there is to read. Confidential discipline records would mean the department is arguing from an incomplete file. Officers being unaware of the standard is an explanation for non-compliance rather than the reason the evidence fails to establish compliance.

questions.stem: The adviser's argument is flawed because:
choices: The previous error may have been minor
Intelligence assessments are inherently uncertain
A source's past error does not establish that the present assessment is wrong
Assessments are produced by teams
questions.explanation: Correct: each assessment rests on its own sources and reasoning, so the earlier failure is a reason for care rather than a ground for dismissal — otherwise no analytic body could ever be believed again. Assessments being inherently uncertain is true of every one of them and singles out nothing about this case. The previous error possibly being minor argues about the severity of the past mistake. Assessments being produced by teams notes that the authorship may differ, which softens the objection without naming the error.

questions.stem: The delegation's argument overlooks the possibility that:
choices: Parties may withhold objections for tactical reasons or lack authority to object
The text may be technically complex
Objections may be raised later
The consultations were poorly attended
questions.explanation: Correct: silence in a negotiation is cheap — a party may be holding its objection for a moment of leverage, waiting on capital, or simply lacking authority to speak — so no objection is not agreement. Poor attendance would explain the silence in one particular way. The text being technically complex suggests objections were missed rather than withheld. Objections being raised later describes what may follow rather than why the present silence proves nothing.

questions.stem: The economist's argument assumes that:
choices: Eight percent is below the regional average
The government has no contingent liabilities
Interest rates and revenue will not change materially
The debt is denominated in domestic currency
questions.explanation: Correct: 8 percent is a ratio between two moving quantities, and refinancing at higher rates or a revenue shortfall would push it up sharply without a cent of new borrowing, so the judgment holds only if both hold roughly steady. Domestic-currency denomination and the absence of contingent liabilities are each one specific way the position could deteriorate, narrower than the assumption the argument needs. The regional average is a comparison the economist never draws.

questions.stem: The analyst's inference is most vulnerable because:
choices: The replacements may be inexperienced
Three ministers is a small number
Reshuffles occur regularly
Personnel changes may serve purposes other than policy change, such as managing coalition politics
questions.explanation: Correct: ministers are moved to satisfy a coalition partner, to answer a scandal, to promote a rival out of the way, or to refresh a tired cabinet, so departures cannot be read straight off as a change of course. Three being a small number quantifies the evidence without addressing what it signifies. The replacements being inexperienced concerns their competence. Reshuffles occurring regularly is closer, but a routine reshuffle could still carry a policy shift; the flaw is reading intent from personnel at all.

questions.stem: The commentator's argument is weakest in that it:
choices: Relies on recent data only
Assumes bilateral and multilateral approaches are substitutes rather than complements
Ignores regional organizations
Does not count the number of agreements
questions.explanation: Correct: states sign bilateral agreements alongside multilateral ones, often to implement or supplement them, so more of the former is evidence of decline only if the two trade off — which the commentator assumes rather than shows. Not counting the agreements asks for numbers that would still not settle the relationship between the two forms. Ignoring regional organizations adds a category to the tally. Relying on recent data questions the time frame rather than the substitution premise.

questions.stem: The official's argument is most vulnerable because:
choices: Two years is a short period
Attendance measures participation rather than any effect on attitudes or behavior
The events may have been poorly organized
Attendance figures may be inflated
questions.explanation: Correct: doubled attendance shows more people came, and the program's aim is presumably to change how they think or act, which a turnstile count cannot register — the same crowd may leave exactly as it arrived. Poorly organized events would suppress attendance rather than explain a rise. Inflated figures question the number itself. Two years being short concerns the window, and the measure would be the wrong one over any period.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most support the policy paper's conclusion?
choices: A state should not accept international obligations that require substantial changes to domestic law
International conventions should be ratified only by supermajority
States should join conventions that most of their neighbors have joined
Domestic law should be amended only when a court requires it
questions.explanation: Correct: the paper's only evidence is the scale of legal change required, so it needs a principle treating that burden as itself decisive — with it, twelve amendments settle the matter without any accounting of benefits. Requiring a supermajority to ratify sets a procedural threshold rather than a reason to decline. Amending domestic law only at a court's direction addresses who may initiate change. Joining what neighbors have joined appeals to regional practice, which the paper never invokes.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most undermine the official's argument?
choices: Aid decisions should be made by recipient governments
Programs should be evaluated by independent auditors
Decisions should be based on expected future costs and benefits, disregarding expenditures already made
Programs should run for a minimum of five years
questions.explanation: Correct: the official's whole case is the money already spent, and a forward-looking principle declares that expenditure irrelevant, leaving the argument with nothing behind it. A five-year minimum would support continuation but on a schedule rather than on the sunk investment. Letting recipient governments decide changes who chooses. Independent evaluation prescribes how to gather evidence, which could cut either way once the evidence arrives and so does not undermine the reasoning itself.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, most supports granting relief?
choices: Partial compliance should be met with proportionate relief to reward progress
Sanctions should never be imposed on states that negotiate
Sanctions should be lifted only on full compliance
Relief decisions should be made multilaterally
questions.explanation: Correct: the specialist needs the conditions to be divisible, and a proportionality principle supplies exactly that, converting three of five into a claim on partial relief. Lifting sanctions only on full compliance is the competing principle that defeats the argument. Never sanctioning states that negotiate would help the target on an entirely different ground the specialist does not raise. Making relief decisions multilaterally concerns who decides rather than what partial compliance earns.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most support the bureau's recommendation?
choices: Reporting quality matters more than quantity
Posts should be maintained in proportion to their measurable reporting output
Resource decisions should be made by the posts themselves
Diplomatic presence should be maintained in every country
questions.explanation: Correct: the bureau ranks posts by cable count and closes the lowest, so it needs a principle tying presence to measurable reporting output — that principle makes the ranking decisive. Maintaining presence in every country forbids closures outright. Letting posts make their own resource decisions changes the decision-maker. Making quality matter more than quantity attacks the bureau's measure and works against the recommendation rather than for it.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most support shortening the training?
choices: Longer training always produces better outcomes
Training decisions should be made by language instructors
Officers should be consulted about training length
Training should be no longer than required to reach the certified proficiency standard
questions.explanation: Correct: both programs reach the certified standard, so a principle that caps training at what the standard requires makes the extra weeks unjustifiable on their own terms. Leaving training decisions to instructors relocates authority. Consulting officers about length adds a procedural step. Saying longer training always produces better outcomes contradicts the premise that both routes arrive at the same proficiency, and would argue for keeping the standard program.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most undermine the official's argument?
choices: Fees should be comparable across posts
Fees should be reviewed every five years
Fee changes require legislative approval
Consular services to citizens abroad should be subsidized rather than priced at cost
questions.explanation: Correct: the official's case rests on fees tracking costs, and a subsidy principle rejects that premise outright — services to citizens abroad would then be priced below cost by design, and fifteen years of unchanged fees is no indictment. Reviewing fees every five years sets a schedule rather than a level. Fee changes needing legislative approval identifies a procedural hurdle. Comparability across posts governs the spread of fees without saying what any of them should recover.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, most supports the study's recommendation?
choices: Where a resource is associated with a desired outcome, increasing the resource is warranted absent evidence of a common cause
Media coverage should not influence budget decisions
Public affairs budgets should be equal across posts
Budgets should be set by host-country conditions
questions.explanation: Correct: the recommendation converts an association into a spending decision, so it needs a principle licensing that move while explicitly setting aside the common-cause worry — which is the objection the study faces. Equal budgets across posts prescribes a distribution unrelated to the finding. Saying coverage should not influence budgets contradicts the recommendation. Setting budgets by host-country conditions offers a different basis for allocation and leaves the study's inference unsupported.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most weaken the economist's conclusion?
choices: Minimum wage policy should be set locally
Employment statistics should be collected quarterly
A policy's effect should be assessed against what would have happened otherwise, not against the prior level
Labor market effects take at least five years to appear
questions.explanation: Correct: the economist compares employment after against employment before, and the principle demands a comparison against the counterfactual — under which flat employment in a growing sector is a loss, and the conclusion collapses. Quarterly statistics concern collection frequency. Setting minimum wage policy locally addresses jurisdiction. Saying effects take five years to appear also undercuts the one-year finding, but it asserts a disputed empirical claim rather than exposing the comparison the economist never made.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, most undermines the evaluation's conclusion?
choices: Participants should not be told the evaluation's purpose
Training programs should be evaluated after one year
Negotiation cannot be taught in a classroom
A program's effect on a skill should be measured by performance rather than by self-assessment
questions.explanation: Correct: the evaluation's only evidence is what graduates say about themselves, and a performance standard rules that out as a measure of skill, leaving the conclusion unsupported. Evaluating after a year changes the timing while permitting the same self-reports. Not telling participants the evaluation's purpose is a design safeguard against bias rather than a rejection of self-assessment. Saying negotiation cannot be taught in a classroom denies the program could ever work, a far stronger claim than the evidence problem at hand.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most undermine the department's projection?
choices: Projections should be revised annually
Digital systems should be introduced gradually
Processing time should be measured from application to decision
Pilot results may be generalized only to populations resembling the pilot population
questions.explanation: Correct: the pilot ran among a highly connected urban population, and a principle restricting generalization to similar populations blocks the extrapolation to applicants who are not — the 40 percent stays where it was measured. Introducing digital systems gradually recommends a rollout pace. Revising projections annually schedules updates rather than challenging this one. Measuring processing time end to end defines the metric, which would apply equally at the pilot post and elsewhere.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most undermine the commentator's argument?
choices: Treaties should be negotiated multilaterally
Binding commitments are valuable when they constrain future governments, not only present ones
Domestic practice should conform to international standards
Compliance should be independently verified
questions.explanation: Correct: the commentator reads present compliance as making the treaty pointless, and this principle identifies the value he has left out — binding a future government that may not share current practice. Negotiating treaties multilaterally concerns procedure. Saying domestic practice should conform to international standards is already satisfied by the parties' compliance and so supports the commentator. Independent verification adds a monitoring requirement rather than a reason to bind.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the researcher's conclusion?
choices: Road construction is expensive
Villages near the road have grown in population
The road was completed five years ago
The road's route was determined by terrain constraints unrelated to village prosperity
questions.explanation: Correct: a route dictated by terrain rather than by which villages looked promising removes the selection problem, making proximity effectively an accident and the income gap attributable to the road. The road being completed five years ago allows time for an effect without showing one occurred. Population growth near the road is consistent with prosperous villages attracting migrants and does not fix the direction. Construction being expensive concerns cost rather than benefit.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the department's claim?
choices: Alumni are surveyed by an independent contractor
The program has operated for thirty years
Applicants rejected for the scholarship report substantially less favorable views a decade later
Most alumni return to their home countries
questions.explanation: Correct: rejected applicants wanted the scholarship too, so they share the initial disposition, and a gap that opens between the two groups a decade later is the program's work rather than the applicants'. Thirty years of operation establishes longevity. An independent contractor conducting the surveys improves their credibility without addressing who was surveyed. Most alumni returning home concerns where the goodwill ends up, which matters to the program's value but not to whether it created the views.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the adviser's claim?
choices: Prohibited items were recovered downstream after passing through the screening point
The procedure has been in place for six months
The procedure requires additional staff
Similar procedures are used at other facilities
questions.explanation: Correct: prohibited items recovered downstream had passed through the screening point, which shows the procedure is missing things and converts the empty log from evidence of success into evidence of blindness. Requiring additional staff concerns cost. Similar procedures being used elsewhere is a fact about other facilities. Six months of operation describes how long the record covers, and a longer empty record would be just as uninformative as a short one.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the analyst's conclusion?
choices: The agreements were mediated by different parties
Power-sharing was adopted only in conflicts involving three or more armed factions
Power-sharing provisions vary in design
Some agreements collapsed after six years
questions.explanation: Correct: if power-sharing appeared only where three or more armed factions were involved, then it marks the most fragmented and hardest conflicts, and the collapses may belong to that difficulty rather than to the clause. Some agreements collapsing after six years concerns cases outside the stated window. Power-sharing provisions varying in design suggests disaggregating them. Different mediators introduces another variable without connecting it to why power-sharing cases failed.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the researcher's conclusion?
choices: Countries that liberalized their press subsequently improved on governance measures, while comparable countries that did not showed no change
Governments in high-ranking countries spend more on public administration
Journalists in low-ranking countries face legal restrictions
Press freedom rankings are compiled by several independent organizations
questions.explanation: Correct: a before-and-after comparison against countries that did not liberalize supplies both a time order and a control, which together rule out the reverse story that effective governments simply tolerate a free press. Multiple organizations compiling the rankings corroborates the measure. Higher administrative spending in top-ranked countries introduces a third variable that could be the real driver. Legal restrictions on journalists in low-ranked countries explains how those rankings arose rather than what press freedom causes.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the department's claim?
choices: The system was adopted at every post simultaneously
Officers rated the system highly in a satisfaction survey
System logs show average time per case fell by a third after the change
Training on the system took two days
questions.explanation: Correct: system logs measure the time actually taken rather than what officers believe about it, which is exactly the weakness in the department's original evidence. A satisfaction survey is another self-report, and a favorable one at that. Simultaneous adoption at every post removes the possibility of a comparison group and makes the claim harder to support. Two days of training describes the cost of switching rather than any saving that followed.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the department's claim?
choices: Fraud detection methods were unchanged
Applications fell at posts without interview requirements too
The share of applications found fraudulent fell by half as well
Interview waiting times increased
questions.explanation: Correct: expressing fraud as a share of applications removes the effect of the halved volume, and a rate falling by half is a real change the shrinking pool cannot explain. Longer interview waits describe a side effect. Applications falling at posts without interviews suggests a common cause for the volume drop, which does nothing for the fraud claim. Unchanged detection methods rules out one alternative but leaves the volume confound entirely in place.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the section's prediction?
choices: The opposition has limited campaign funding
The electoral commission has since been reconstituted on terms the opposition demanded
The opposition's leadership has not changed
Turnout in the previous elections was low
questions.explanation: Correct: reconstituting the commission on the opposition's own terms removes the grievance the boycotts were built on, which is precisely the condition the prediction quietly assumes persists. Unchanged leadership supports the prediction rather than weakening it. Low turnout in the previous elections describes their result. Limited campaign funding gives the opposition a practical reason to sit out, which again strengthens the case for another boycott.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the analyst's inference?
choices: Two other ministers were also moved between portfolios
The reshuffle occurred at the usual point in the electoral cycle
The three replacements have each publicly criticized the previous approach
The prime minister described the changes as routine
questions.explanation: Correct: replacements who have publicly attacked the previous approach connect the personnel change to policy directly, closing the gap between a reshuffle and a shift in direction. The reshuffle occurring at the usual point in the cycle suggests routine timing and works against the inference. The prime minister calling the changes routine cuts against it more explicitly still. Two other ministers being moved between portfolios adds churn without indicating any direction.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the official's claim?
choices: The events received local press coverage
Surveys of attendees show sustained shifts in views on the sponsoring country
Attendance grew fastest among students
Event costs per attendee fell
questions.explanation: Correct: sustained shifts in attendees' views measure the outcome the program exists to produce, which attendance alone can never show. Falling cost per attendee improves efficiency at delivering the same unmeasured thing. Local press coverage extends the program's reach, again without evidence of effect. Attendance growing fastest among students describes the composition of the crowd, which may matter for targeting but still counts bodies rather than change.

questions.stem: If both the fraud figure and the volume figure are accurate, which is best supported?
choices: The interview requirement had no effect
The fraud rate fell
The fraud rate rose
Whether the fraud rate changed cannot be determined from the figures given
questions.explanation: Correct: fraud counts fell and applications halved, and without the two numbers expressed against each other the rate could have risen, fallen, or held steady — the figures given are simply insufficient. Saying the requirement had no effect asserts one of those possibilities. Saying the rate rose picks another, and saying it fell picks the third; each states a conclusion the arithmetic leaves open.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best supported?
choices: The record is consistent with both full compliance and absent enforcement
Officers have complied with the standard
The standard is poorly drafted
The standard is not being enforced
questions.explanation: Correct: a standard perfectly observed and a standard never enforced generate the same empty disciplinary record, so the evidence fits both stories equally and settles neither. Concluding officers have complied is the department's own overreach. Concluding the standard is not enforced overreaches in the other direction with no more support. Calling the standard poorly drafted introduces a defect in the text that the disciplinary record says nothing about.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best supported by the economist's observation?
choices: The trading partner's currency is undervalued
The country's exports are uncompetitive
Prices for the sampled goods differ substantially between the two countries
The currency will depreciate
questions.explanation: Correct: the observation is a measured price difference for the sampled basket, and that is what it establishes — the leap to overvaluation requires further assumptions about tradability that the figure alone does not supply. Predicting depreciation forecasts a market movement. Calling exports uncompetitive draws a consequence that depends on which goods are traded. Saying the partner's currency is undervalued relabels the same gap from the other side and is equally unsupported.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best supported?
choices: A communiqué was drafted but rejected
The summit did not produce a communiqué
The parties disagreed on every issue
The summit failed
questions.explanation: Correct: the one thing the stimulus establishes is the absence of a communiqué; the commentator's verdict is the inference under challenge, not a fact to be inherited. Saying the summit failed adopts that verdict. Saying the parties disagreed on every issue explains the absence in the most extreme way available. Saying a communiqué was drafted but rejected invents a specific history the stimulus never describes.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best supported?
choices: This coalition has lasted longer than the historical average
Most coalitions collapse before twenty months
This coalition will collapse soon
This coalition is unusually stable
questions.explanation: Correct: twenty months against an eighteen-month average is a straightforward comparison of two numbers, and it is all the premises deliver. Predicting imminent collapse is the analyst's inference, which the dispersion around an average does not license. Calling the coalition unusually stable overreads a two-month margin. Saying most coalitions collapse before twenty months treats the mean as a median, and a few very long coalitions could produce that average with most lasting longer.

questions.stem: Which of the following must be true?
choices: The remaining conditions are more difficult than the first three
The target government has not met two of the specified conditions
The target government intends to meet the remaining conditions
Relief will be granted
questions.explanation: Correct: five conditions were specified and three met, so exactly two remain unmet — arithmetic, and nothing more. Attributing an intention to meet the rest reads a plan into a count. Saying the remaining conditions are harder ranks their difficulty with nothing to go on. Saying relief will be granted predicts the decision, which is the very thing the specialist is arguing for rather than something the facts establish.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best supported?
choices: The government could borrow substantially more
The debt will remain manageable
Interest payments currently consume a modest share of revenue
The debt is denominated in domestic currency
questions.explanation: Correct: the 8 percent figure describes the present burden, and that is what it supports; the economist's leap to manageability depends on the ratio staying put. Saying the debt will remain manageable makes that leap. Saying the government could borrow substantially more draws a policy conclusion about headroom. Saying the debt is domestically denominated adds a fact about its composition that the revenue share does not reveal.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best supported?
choices: War would impose severe economic costs on both governments
Economic interdependence prevents war
The two governments will not go to war
Neither government wants war
questions.explanation: Correct: the cost premise is what the specialist asserts and the prediction is what he infers from it, so the costs are the supported part. Saying the two will not go to war adopts the conclusion under challenge. Saying interdependence prevents war generalizes that conclusion into a law. Saying neither government wants war attributes preferences, when a government may want a war it knows would be ruinous.

questions.stem: The analyst's argument assumes that:
choices: Exports drove GDP rather than moving with it as one of its components
Export prices were stable
GDP is measured at constant prices
Imports remained constant
questions.explanation: Correct: exports are a component of GDP, so they rise with it almost mechanically, and the argument works only if exports are pulling output rather than being carried along by a domestic expansion. Constant imports would matter to the trade balance rather than to the direction of causation. Stable export prices concerns whether volumes or values moved. Constant-price GDP measurement guards against inflation distorting both series alike.

questions.stem: The adviser's argument assumes that:
choices: Currency instability is easy to detect
The next crisis will resemble the last three in its origins
Exchange rate data are published promptly
Other indicators are more expensive to monitor
questions.explanation: Correct: the recommendation to watch exchange rates is efficient only if the next crisis starts where the last three did; one beginning in a border dispute or a succession would develop unwatched. Prompt publication of currency data concerns the timeliness of the indicator. Currency instability being easy to detect concerns its visibility. Other indicators being more expensive would support choosing this one on cost, which is a different argument from the one the adviser makes.

questions.stem: The analyst's argument assumes that:
choices: Turnout was high
The stations observers visited were representative of all polling stations
Voting was conducted by secret ballot
Observers were impartial
questions.explanation: Correct: the observers saw a subset, and the conclusion covers the whole election, so the argument stands or falls on whether that subset reflected the rest — stations chosen for accessibility often do not. Observer impartiality bears on whether their reports are trustworthy, which the argument also needs but which is not the gap between subset and whole. Secret ballot concerns the voting method. High turnout describes participation rather than integrity.

questions.stem: The department's argument assumes that:
choices: Participants took the assessment seriously
Corruption is a serious problem in the department
The assessment was administered fairly
Assessment scores predict conduct
questions.explanation: Correct: the department infers effective training from a rising score, which requires the score to stand in for conduct — and knowing the right answer under examination is not the same as choosing it under pressure. Participants taking the assessment seriously and the assessment being administered fairly are conditions for the score being meaningful at all, narrower than the link to behavior. Corruption being a serious problem is the reason for running the training rather than a premise that it worked.

questions.stem: The commentator's argument assumes that:
choices: Multilateral institutions were once more effective
Bilateral agreements are easier to negotiate
Bilateral activity comes at the expense of multilateral engagement
States prefer bilateral arrangements
questions.explanation: Correct: more bilateral activity signals multilateral decline only if the two compete for the same effort; if states pursue both, or use bilateral deals to implement multilateral commitments, the trend shows nothing about decline. Bilateral agreements being easier to negotiate would explain why states favor them without establishing the trade-off. Multilateral institutions once being more effective is a claim about the past the commentator would need to argue separately. States preferring bilateral arrangements restates the observed behavior rather than supplying the missing link.

questions.stem: The delegation's argument assumes that:
choices: Consultations were conducted in a common language
A party that finds the text unacceptable would have said so during consultation
All parties attended the consultations
The text has not been revised
questions.explanation: Correct: silence counts as consent only if an unhappy party would have spoken, so the argument rests entirely on the consultations being a forum where objections actually surface. All parties attending and a common language are conditions that make speaking possible, each narrower than the willingness the argument needs. The text not having been revised concerns whether the silence attaches to the current draft, which is a question about what was consulted on rather than about what silence means.

questions.stem: The official's argument assumes that:
choices: The majority is well informed
Opponents will accept the outcome
Majority support is sufficient to justify a policy
The polling was methodologically sound
questions.explanation: Correct: the argument offers popular support and stops, so it needs that support to be enough on its own — without sufficiency, a large majority is a political fact rather than a justification. Sound polling methodology would establish that the majority exists, which the official takes as given. The majority being well informed would make the support more creditable but is not what the inference turns on. Opponents accepting the outcome concerns compliance after the decision rather than its justification.

questions.stem: The department's projection assumes that:
choices: The system will not require maintenance
Processing time is the only relevant measure
Applicants elsewhere will adopt the digital system at rates comparable to the pilot population
Staff will need no additional training
questions.explanation: Correct: the pilot's 40 percent was produced by a population that could actually use the digital channel, so projecting it elsewhere assumes comparable take-up — where connectivity or digital literacy is thinner, applications revert to paper and the saving evaporates. The system requiring no maintenance and staff needing no extra training are operating costs that would reduce the net benefit without touching the extrapolation. Processing time being the only relevant measure concerns what else matters, not whether this measure travels.

questions.stem: The official's argument assumes that:
choices: The drawbacks cannot be mitigated
All alternatives have been identified
Doing nothing is not an option
The proposed policy's drawbacks are less serious than those of the alternatives
questions.explanation: Correct: showing that every alternative is flawed leaves the field level unless the proposal's own drawbacks are lighter, so that comparison is the load-bearing premise the official never states. All alternatives having been identified would make the survey complete without ranking anything. Doing nothing not being an option removes one further alternative. The drawbacks being unmitigable applies to the proposal and the alternatives alike and so does not settle the comparison either.

questions.stem: The delegation's argument assumes that:
choices: Moderation is desirable in negotiation
The other two positions define a reasonable range
Its own position was formulated first
The other parties negotiated independently
questions.explanation: Correct: a midpoint inherits its character from the endpoints, so calling the proposal moderate presupposes that the two flanking positions mark out a sensible span — between two extremes, the middle is extreme too. The other parties negotiating independently would prevent them from bracketing the delegation deliberately, a narrower worry. The delegation's position being formulated first concerns the order of drafting. Moderation being desirable explains why the label is worth claiming rather than whether it applies.

questions.stem: Which additional premise would allow the conclusion that some working group members have doctoral degrees?
choices: The working group includes non-economists
Some economists lack doctoral degrees
All department staff have doctoral degrees
The working group's economists are department economists
questions.explanation: Correct: the doctoral premise covers only economists in the department, so placing the working group's economists there closes the gap and the conclusion follows. Saying all department staff hold doctorates broadens the premise but still never connects the working group to the department. Saying some economists lack doctorates weakens the chain. Saying the working group includes non-economists describes its other members and bears on nothing in the inference.

questions.stem: Which of the following would most help determine whether inflation fell in Country K?
choices: The average inflation decline among adopters
Country K's inflation data for the past three years
The number of countries that adopted the reform
Whether Country K's neighbors adopted the reform
questions.explanation: Correct: the question is what happened in one country, and its own inflation series answers it directly rather than by inference from a majority. The number of adopters describes the size of the group behind the generalization. The average decline among adopters describes the typical case, which is what already made this only probable. Whether K's neighbors adopted the reform concerns other countries entirely and would leave K's own experience unknown.

questions.stem: Which of the following would most undermine the force of the conclusion about the fisheries agreement?
choices: Time pressure is common in negotiations
The relevant government is not expected to change
Some agreements reached without time pressure have also collapsed
The fisheries agreement is unusually detailed
questions.explanation: Correct: the generalization fires only at a change of government, so if none is expected the prediction has no occasion to come true and its practical force drains away. Agreements without time pressure also collapsing concerns a different category and leaves this rule intact. The agreement being unusually detailed suggests it might be an exception without giving any reason it would be. Time pressure being common in negotiations widens the rule's reach rather than blunting it.

questions.stem: Which of the following would most weaken any expectation that the pending treaty will be ratified?
choices: The pending treaty is lengthy
The Senate has rejected few treaties overall
Bipartisan sponsorship has become more common
Several treaties with bipartisan sponsorship have also been rejected
questions.explanation: Correct: bipartisan treaties having been rejected too shows the feature does not protect against rejection, so its presence here supports no expectation of ratification. The Senate having rejected few treaties overall makes rejection rare and so favors the treaty's chances. Bipartisan sponsorship becoming more common would dilute its significance but only indirectly. The treaty being lengthy is a fact about the text with no established bearing on its fate.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the adviser's argument?
choices: Agencies are legally required to follow procedures that firms may disregard
Performance management systems vary widely among firms
Some private firms are inefficient
Government salaries are lower than private sector salaries
questions.explanation: Correct: if agencies must follow procedures firms may ignore, the efficiency gap is produced by the legal environment rather than by management, and importing the practices would leave the constraints untouched. Some firms being inefficient notes exceptions to a stated general comparison. Lower government salaries offer a separate explanation for the gap, but one that would argue for changing pay rather than for keeping the practices out. Performance systems varying among firms complicates which practices to copy.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the officer's assessment?
choices: The source's reporting has been independently corroborated on four separate occasions
The information is consistent with the officer's expectations
The source has reported for many years
The source has no known political affiliation
questions.explanation: Correct: four independent corroborations turn a single past success into a pattern verified from outside, which is exactly what the officer's one-case argument lacks. Reporting for many years measures tenure rather than accuracy. No known political affiliation removes one motive to deceive without evidencing accuracy. The information matching the officer's expectations is the weakest of all, since agreeable reporting is what a fabricator would supply.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the adviser's position?
choices: Assessments are reviewed before distribution
The earlier assessment concerned a different country
The assessment team has been reorganized
The current assessment rests on the same analytic method that produced the earlier error
questions.explanation: Correct: if the current assessment uses the method that produced the earlier failure, the past error becomes evidence about this product rather than a fact about the analysts' record — a defect in the method carries forward. The earlier assessment concerning a different country reduces the relevance of the precedent. The team having been reorganized suggests a different set of judgments is now involved. Assessments being reviewed before distribution describes a safeguard, which again cuts against the adviser.

questions.stem: Which of the following most closely parallels the officer's reasoning?
choices: Defendants usually plead not guilty, so this defendant's plea tells us nothing about guilt
Most reports are accurate, so this report is accurate
The allegation is serious, so it is probably true
This witness lied once, so nothing the witness says can be believed
questions.explanation: Correct: pleading not guilty is what nearly all defendants do, so it carries no information about this one — the same structure as denials being routine and therefore uninformative about this denial. Saying a witness who lied once can never be believed generalizes from one instance to a person's whole testimony, which is a different error. Saying most reports are accurate so this one is applies a base rate to a case rather than declining to. Saying a serious allegation is probably true infers truth from gravity.

questions.stem: Which of the following most closely parallels the official's reasoning?
choices: We enjoyed the last performance, so we should attend this one
We have already paid for the tickets, so we should attend the performance despite the storm warning
Attending would cost more than staying home
The performance received poor reviews, so we should not attend
questions.explanation: Correct: money spent on tickets is gone whether one attends or not, so it cannot make attending in a storm the better choice — precisely the official's move of treating past expenditure as a reason to continue. Declining because of poor reviews weighs a forward-looking consideration. Attending because the last performance was enjoyable reasons from past experience to expected value, which is legitimate. Comparing the cost of attending with staying home weighs future costs, which is exactly what the sunk-cost reasoner fails to do.

questions.stem: Which of the following most closely parallels the adviser's reasoning?
choices: The alarm is new, so it is reliable
The alarm was tested last week and worked
The smoke alarm sounded, so there is a fire
The smoke alarm has never sounded, so it must be working
questions.explanation: Correct: an alarm that has never sounded may be watching a house that has never burned or may be dead on the wall, which is the adviser's silence read as success. An alarm sounding taken as proof of fire affirms the consequent instead. Calling a new alarm reliable infers from its age. An alarm tested last week and found working is the sound version of the argument — a positive check rather than an inference from silence.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most undermine the department's inference?
choices: A compliance record is informative only where a functioning detection mechanism exists
Officers should be trained on new standards
Discipline should be proportionate to the violation
Conduct standards should be reviewed periodically
questions.explanation: Correct: it identifies exactly what the department's record lacks — without a mechanism that would catch violations, an empty disciplinary file carries no information about conduct. Reviewing standards periodically prescribes maintenance of the rule. Proportionate discipline governs the severity of penalties once imposed. Training officers on new standards would improve compliance and, if anything, offers a further reason to expect the standard is observed rather than undermining the inference from the record.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most undermine the official's claim?
choices: A program should be judged by its effect on its intended outcome, not by participation levels
Attendance should be recorded accurately
Programs should be evaluated by external reviewers
Outreach events should be held quarterly
questions.explanation: Correct: the official's evidence is participation, and this principle rules participation out as the test, leaving the doubled attendance with nothing to prove. Holding events quarterly prescribes a schedule. External reviewers change who evaluates rather than what counts as success. Accurate attendance records would make the official's number trustworthy, which strengthens the evidence he has instead of showing it is the wrong evidence.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, most supports the commentator's conclusion?
choices: Nominees should be confirmed by the Senate
Language ability should be required for all diplomatic posts
Ambassadors should be career officers
Regional experience is indispensable to effective performance as an ambassador
questions.explanation: Correct: the commentator infers unfitness from one missing credential, which follows only if that credential is indispensable — the principle supplies exactly that. Requiring ambassadors to be career officers rests on a different qualification the commentator never raises. Senate confirmation concerns the appointment process. Requiring language ability for all diplomatic posts imposes a related but distinct condition, and an ambassador could satisfy it while still lacking regional experience.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most undermine the commentator's argument?
choices: Foreign policy should prioritize national interest
Self-determination is a settled principle of international law
Applying different principles to materially different situations is consistent rather than incoherent
States should apply the same rule to allies and adversaries
questions.explanation: Correct: the charge of incoherence depends on the two cases being alike, and this principle denies that differently situated cases must be treated the same, which removes the contradiction. Prioritising national interest would explain the divergence as self-interested rather than principled, conceding the inconsistency. Applying the same rule to allies and adversaries supports the commentator. Calling self-determination a settled principle strengthens the objection to withholding it in the second region.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most undermine the researcher's argument?
choices: Legitimacy requires democratic accountability
States should comply with all rulings
An institution is legitimate if its rulings are generally accepted as authoritative, whether or not compliance is costly in each case
International courts should have compulsory jurisdiction
questions.explanation: Correct: the researcher measures legitimacy by compliance under cost, and this principle relocates it to general acceptance of authority, so convenient compliance no longer condemns the courts. Compulsory jurisdiction proposes an institutional reform. Saying states should comply with all rulings endorses the standard the researcher applies. Requiring democratic accountability introduces a different objection to the courts' legitimacy and so works alongside the researcher rather than against.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, most supports the negotiator's inference?
choices: Negotiators should always explain position changes
Domestic politics shapes all foreign policy
Hardened positions indicate bad faith
A party that hardens its position without new substantive justification is responding to pressures outside the negotiation
questions.explanation: Correct: the negotiator reads an unexplained hardening as a sign of domestic pressure, and only a principle linking that behavior to outside pressures licenses the step from conduct to cause. Saying negotiators should always explain position changes states an expectation about conduct rather than what a breach signifies. Domestic politics shaping all foreign policy is too broad to single out this delegation's move. Hardened positions indicating bad faith supplies a different diagnosis altogether and would undercut the pressure reading.

questions.stem: Which of the following must be true?
choices: Country M meets all requirements for membership
Some bloc members retain agricultural tariffs
Country M will eventually join the trade bloc
Eliminating agricultural tariffs is not sufficient for membership in the trade bloc
questions.explanation: Correct: M has eliminated the tariffs without being a member, which is precisely a case of the condition holding while membership does not — so elimination cannot be sufficient. Predicting M will join adds a forecast the premises never license. Saying M meets all requirements assumes tariffs are the only requirement, when the stimulus establishes only that members share this one feature. Saying some members retain tariffs contradicts the premise that all have eliminated them.

questions.stem: Which of the following can be properly concluded?
choices: The literacy project is more likely to be funded than unevaluated projects
The department funds all evaluated projects
The literacy project has satisfied a necessary condition for funding
The department will fund the literacy project
questions.explanation: Correct: 'only if' states a necessary condition, so evaluation is a hurdle cleared and nothing more. Concluding the department will fund the project affirms the consequent, treating a hurdle as a guarantee. Calling funding more likely than for unevaluated projects sounds moderate but still overreaches: unevaluated projects are ruled out entirely, which fixes their odds without fixing this project's. Saying the department funds all evaluated projects converts the necessary condition into a sufficient one outright.

questions.stem: Which of the following must be true?
choices: Country R will be sanctioned
Country R intends to ratify the protocol later
Country R has not ratified the protocol
Ratifying the protocol prevents emissions from rising
questions.explanation: Correct: no ratifier has been permitted to increase, and R has been permitted, so R cannot be among the ratifiers — a valid denial of the consequent. Predicting sanctions introduces a penalty the stimulus never mentions. Attributing an intention to ratify later reads a plan into a fact about R's current status. Saying ratification prevents emissions from rising confuses the allocation rule with actual emissions, which may rise or fall within any allocation.

questions.stem: The official's argument is most vulnerable to the criticism that:
choices: Some officers have medical restrictions
Hardship posts are more expensive to staff
Career satisfaction is difficult to measure
Officers who volunteer for hardship posts may differ from those who would be compelled to serve
questions.explanation: Correct: volunteers chose the hardship post, and whatever disposition led them to choose it plausibly also produces their satisfaction, so the outcome may not survive compulsion — the very change the recommendation proposes. Hardship posts being expensive to staff is a budget consideration. Career satisfaction being hard to measure adds noise to the finding without explaining why compelled officers would respond differently. Medical restrictions identify officers who cannot serve, a practical limit on implementing the rule rather than a flaw in the inference.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Compliance will certainly improve within a year
Publishing findings is the only way to improve compliance
Compliance would not have improved without publication
Based on the past pattern, compliance can reasonably be expected to improve
questions.explanation: Correct: an unbroken run of past cases warrants an expectation without guaranteeing the next one, since the stimulus reports a regularity rather than stating a law. Certainty overreads that record. Calling publication the only route to improved compliance converts a sufficient condition into a necessary one, when other measures may work just as well. Saying compliance would not have improved without publication asserts a counterfactual the stimulus never tests — improvement within a year is consistent with causes the publication merely accompanied.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the economist's argument?
choices: Air quality is measured at three monitoring stations
Fuel subsidies had been in place for over a decade
A large coal-fired plant on the city's edge closed permanently in the same month
Subsidy removal was unpopular with urban residents
questions.explanation: Correct: a large coal plant closing in the same month supplies a cause big enough to produce the improvement on its own, leaving the subsidy removal with nothing to explain. Subsidies having been in place for a decade describes the policy's history. Their removal being unpopular concerns the politics rather than the air. Measuring at three stations is a limitation of the monitoring network that would affect readings before and after alike, so it cannot account for a change between them.

questions.stem: The director's reasoning is most vulnerable because:
choices: Some graduates do not take the examination
Non-graduates may have studied independently
Competitive admission means graduates already outperformed others before enrolling
The certification examination may be poorly designed
questions.explanation: Correct: admission selects on prior examination performance, so graduates were already the stronger test-takers and would have outscored non-graduates with no curriculum at all — the gap is built into who gets in. A poorly designed examination would distort both groups' scores equally. Some graduates not sitting the examination is a small gap in coverage. Non-graduates studying independently would, if anything, narrow the gap and make the institute's result more impressive rather than less.

questions.stem: The commentator's argument is flawed because it:
choices: Relies on an arbitrarily chosen six-month period
Treats the absence of fighting as evidence that the cause of the fighting has ended
Assumes ceasefires are always formally negotiated
Ignores the role of external mediators
questions.explanation: Correct: fighting can stop because a dispute was settled or because it is being held down by exhaustion, deterrence, or outside pressure, so quiet on the ground says nothing about the politics beneath it. Calling six months arbitrary is related but weaker: the same inference would fail at any length. Assuming ceasefires are formally negotiated concerns how they come about. Ignoring external mediators points to one particular alternative explanation rather than naming the error in the inference itself.

questions.stem: If the auditor's observation is accurate, the reported coverage figure is unreliable because:
choices: Census data are collected for other purposes
Migration makes the campaign harder to administer
Vaccination records may be incomplete
The denominator understates the current target population
questions.explanation: Correct: coverage is a fraction, and a twelve-year-old count taken before substantial in-migration puts too small a number underneath it, so the true share reached is lower than 85 percent. Incomplete vaccination records would corrupt the numerator, which is not what the auditor identified. Migration making administration harder is an operational difficulty rather than a measurement error. Census data being collected for other purposes is true of most official statistics and does not by itself make them wrong here.

questions.stem: The analyst's argument assumes that:
choices: The agency's staff are competent
Prosecution volume is a valid indicator of the agency's effectiveness
Corruption is more prevalent than official figures suggest
The agency has adequate funding
questions.explanation: Correct: falling prosecutions are read straight off as failure, which holds only if the count tracks performance — yet a successful agency may deter wrongdoing, or trade many weak cases for a few strong ones. Adequate funding bears on why the agency might underperform rather than on whether the measure is sound. Corruption being worse than official figures suggest is a claim about the underlying problem. Staff competence is another possible cause of poor results, not a premise the inference rests on.

questions.stem: The colleague's observation undermines the diplomat's claim by suggesting that:
choices: The parties negotiated in bad faith
The summit was too short to accomplish anything
Communiqués are not legally binding
The communiqué produced no change in any party's position
questions.explanation: Correct: if the communiqué restates commitments already made in public, nothing moved, and a signature ratifying the status quo cannot show the summit achieved anything. Saying the parties negotiated in bad faith imputes intent the observation does not support; they may have tried and failed. Saying the summit was too short offers a cause for the emptiness rather than establishing it. Noting that communiqués are not legally binding is generally true and would apply equally to a communiqué full of genuine concessions.

questions.stem: The administrator's conclusion is most vulnerable to the objection that:
choices: Some study-abroad programs are more rigorous than others
Salaries vary widely by field of study
A decade is too short a period to assess earnings
Students who study abroad may differ in family resources and prior attainment
questions.explanation: Correct: students who go abroad tend to come from families that can pay for it and to have stronger records already, and those advantages produce higher salaries on their own — so expanding access to different students need not reproduce the gap. Salaries varying by field is a reason to control the comparison. A decade being too short would understate any effect rather than manufacture one. Programs differing in rigour concerns which version to expand, not whether expansion would raise earnings at all.

questions.stem: The official's proposal assumes that:
choices: Large grantees are more experienced
Small grants have never achieved their objectives
Administrative efficiency is the appropriate basis for choosing grant size
Administrative costs will continue to rise
questions.explanation: Correct: the proposal ranks grants by cost of administration alone, which decides the question only if nothing else about a grant counts — small grants may reach applicants and problems large ones cannot. Saying small grants have never achieved their objectives is far stronger than the argument needs and is not claimed. Large grantees being more experienced offers a further reason to favor them that the official does not use. Administrative costs continuing to rise concerns future budgets rather than the comparison being drawn.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, most supports the civil liberties group's position?
choices: A program that restricts liberty is justified only if less restrictive means would not have achieved the same result
Disrupting plots is the primary measure of a security program's value
Intelligence methods should be disclosed to the public
Security programs should be discontinued whenever they are controversial
questions.explanation: Correct: the group's whole point is that the four disruptions prove nothing until alternatives are ruled out, so it needs a least-restrictive-means standard that makes that comparison decisive. Discontinuing programs whenever they are controversial rests the case on public opinion rather than on the necessity the group actually raised. Disclosing intelligence methods is a transparency demand about a different subject. Making plot disruption the primary measure of value hands the argument to the security service.

questions.stem: The specialist's reasoning is most vulnerable because:
choices: Formal negotiations are often preceded by informal contacts
Governments change for many reasons
The specialist has not identified which government changed
The change of government may have coincided with other shifts that made negotiation possible
questions.explanation: Correct: governments change amid other upheavals — a shifting balance of power, economic pressure, a change in a third state's posture — any of which could open negotiations without the old government having been the obstacle. Informal contacts preceding formal talks refines when the process really began. Governments changing for many reasons is true but does not connect to the negotiations. Not identifying which government changed is a gap in the telling rather than in the reasoning.

questions.stem: The donor's recommendation is most vulnerable to the objection that:
choices: Clinic B is smaller and may lack capacity to expand
Clinic B may achieve its rate by treating less severe cases
Recovery rates fluctuate month to month
Clinic A employs more staff
questions.explanation: Correct: a clinic taking easier cases will post a better recovery rate while doing less good, so the two rates are not comparable until case mix is known — and the smaller clinic is the likelier one to be selecting. Clinic A employing more staff describes its scale. Month-to-month fluctuation adds noise to both figures alike. Clinic B lacking capacity to expand is a genuine practical objection to redirecting funds, but it concedes the quality comparison instead of challenging it.

questions.stem: The policy paper's reasoning is flawed because it:
choices: Ignores transitions outside the region
Treats a feature common to past successes as a requirement for future ones
Does not define democratic transition
Relies on too few cases
questions.explanation: Correct: every past success sharing a feature does not make that feature required — the successes may simply be the cases where growth happened to be present, and a transition without it would go unrepresented in a sample built only from successes. Relying on too few cases disputes the sample size, whereas the error would persist with hundreds. Not defining democratic transition makes the claim imprecise. Ignoring transitions outside the region asks for more cases rather than exposing the logical leap.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the officer's conclusion?
choices: The officer helped design the template
Washington's rating scale was unchanged
The new front office substantially revised cables before transmission
The template was adopted at several other posts
questions.explanation: Correct: a front office rewriting cables before transmission means Washington was rating the revisions, so the improvement may be entirely the editing and not the template — the two arrived together and the ratings cannot separate them. Adoption at other posts would be evidence to gather, not a weakness here. The rating scale being unchanged removes one alternative explanation and so mildly strengthens the claim. The officer having designed the template raises a question about her motives rather than about the evidence.

questions.stem: The information about vehicle registrations undermines the ministry's claim by suggesting that:
choices: Traffic fatalities are poorly recorded
Fatalities may have fallen because there were fewer vehicles on the road
The fuel price increase was more unpopular than the campaign
The campaign was too short to have an effect
questions.explanation: Correct: fewer registered vehicles means fewer vehicles in traffic, and a 22 percent drop in exposure comfortably accounts for an 18 percent drop in deaths with no contribution from the campaign. The fuel price increase being unpopular concerns its politics. Poorly recorded fatalities would undermine the number itself, which is not what the registration figure shows.
