The campaign being too short proposes a reason it might have failed rather than explaining why the evidence of success is illusory.

questions.stem: The negotiator's argument assumes that:
choices: The earlier agreement was fully implemented
Both sides value the agreement equally
The other side's circumstances and alternatives have not materially changed since the earlier talks
The other side negotiates in good faith
questions.explanation: Correct: the inference from a better offer to acceptance holds only if the other side's position is the same one that made the earlier offer acceptable; three years can change their alternatives, their leadership, or their need, and 'better' is judged against those. Good faith concerns how they negotiate rather than what they will accept. Implementation of the earlier agreement is a separate question about the past. Both sides valuing the agreement equally is neither claimed nor needed.

questions.stem: The analyst's recommendation is most vulnerable to the objection that:
choices: Countries that sign such treaties may already be those investors find attractive
Investment treaties constrain domestic regulatory authority
Treaty texts vary considerably
Not all foreign investment benefits recipients
questions.explanation: Correct: stable, growing economies with sound institutions are both likelier to sign treaties and likelier to attract capital, so the treaty may be a marker of investor appeal rather than a cause of it — signing would then change nothing for a country lacking those traits. Treaties constraining regulatory authority is a cost worth weighing, but it grants that they draw investment. Not all investment benefiting recipients questions the goal. Varying treaty texts is a reason to look at particular provisions.

questions.stem: The director's response is weak because:
choices: The inspector general has broader authority than the director
An absence of detected incidents does not establish that procedures are adequate
Written procedures are required by regulation
Eleven years is a short period
questions.explanation: Correct: with no written procedure and no monitoring described, a clean record is as consistent with lucky and undetected mishandling as with sound practice, so it cannot establish adequacy. Calling eleven years short concedes that the record would count for something at a greater length, when the problem is what it can show at any length. Written procedures being required by regulation is a reason to have one but does not answer the director's evidential claim. The inspector general's authority concerns who may raise the finding.

questions.stem: The commentator's argument is most vulnerable to the criticism that it:
choices: Assumes household income is the only relevant outcome
Relies on evaluators who may be biased
Ignores the program's administrative costs
Treats a failure to detect an effect as a demonstration that no effect exists
questions.explanation: Correct: a null result is compatible with a real but modest effect, a noisy measure, or an underpowered study, so it establishes that no effect was found rather than that none exists. Evaluator bias questions the evaluation's integrity, whereas the stimulus presents it as independent. Ignoring administrative costs would matter to a value-for-money verdict the commentator is not delivering. Assuming income is the only relevant outcome is a real limitation, but the misreading of the null finding is the error inside the inference.

questions.stem: The adviser's argument is weakest in that it:
choices: Generalizes from three cases without considering how many private-sector appointees were ineffective
Does not define private-sector experience
Assumes ambassadorial effectiveness can be ranked
Ignores the role of career officers
questions.explanation: Correct: three effective ambassadors from business tell you nothing without the denominator — if fifty private-sector appointees served and forty-seven struggled, the same three cases would remain true while the recommendation collapsed. Assuming effectiveness can be ranked questions the premise's measurement. Ignoring career officers names a group left out of the comparison rather than the sampling error. Not defining private-sector experience leaves the recruiting criterion vague, which affects implementation rather than the inference.

questions.stem: The projection's stated assumption is questionable primarily because:
choices: The reform may not be enacted
Revenue projections are inherently uncertain
Taxpayers commonly adjust reported income and timing in response to rate changes
Six percent is a small increase
questions.explanation: Correct: rates change incentives, and taxpayers respond by shifting the timing of income, recharacterising it, or reporting less, so a projection freezing behavior will misstate revenue in a predictable direction. Projections being inherently uncertain is true of all of them and identifies no particular defect. The reform possibly not being enacted concerns whether the projection ever applies. Six percent being a small increase comments on the magnitude claimed rather than on the assumption behind it.

questions.stem: The researcher's conclusion confuses:
choices: Correlation with sample size
The incidence of corruption with the reporting of corruption
Government corruption with private corruption
Press freedom with press quality
questions.explanation: Correct: a free press produces reports, and more reports of corruption are exactly what one expects when detection improves rather than when wrongdoing increases — the measure counts visibility, not conduct. Confusing correlation with sample size misnames the error; the sample is not the issue. Confusing press freedom with press quality substitutes one press variable for another without touching what is being counted. Distinguishing government from private corruption narrows the subject matter but leaves the reporting-versus-incidence problem exactly as it was.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best supported by the economic section's observation?
choices: The host country's economy is not actually growing
The host government is deliberately falsifying data
The reported figures are implausibly stable for an economy of this kind
Growth is lower than 7 percent
questions.explanation: Correct: the observation is about the shape of the series — nine years inside a fifth of a point, which economies of this kind do not manage — so what it supports is that the numbers look too smooth to be real. Concluding the economy is not growing goes far beyond it; a real 5 percent could be smoothed into a fake 7. Concluding the government is deliberately falsifying data attributes intent, when incompetence or a bad methodology would look the same. Concluding growth is below 7 picks a direction the evidence does not indicate.

questions.stem: The official's argument overlooks the possibility that:
choices: Some cases settle before hearing
The arbitration panel may be biased
The department has brought few cases
The department may decline to bring cases it expects to lose
questions.explanation: Correct: if the department screens out cases it expects to lose, the perfect record reflects which cases were brought rather than how sound its positions are — the losses simply never enter the sample. A biased panel would explain the wins but is an accusation the stimulus gives no basis for. Cases settling before hearing narrows what the record covers without explaining the selection. Having brought few cases makes the record thin, yet even a long record built by the same screening would prove no more.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the study's attribution?
choices: Officers who remain past three years are disproportionately assigned to lower-risk applicant pools
Local knowledge is difficult to quantify
Refusal rates vary across posts
Some officers extend their tours voluntarily
questions.explanation: Correct: if the longer-serving officers handle safer applicant pools, the 6-point gap comes from the caseload rather than from anything they learned, and local knowledge does no work in the explanation. Refusal rates varying across posts is a reason to compare within a post. Local knowledge being hard to quantify makes the causal claim hard to test rather than showing it is wrong. Officers extending voluntarily hints at selection, but volunteering says nothing about which applicants they then see.

questions.stem: The commentator's argument is most vulnerable to the criticism that it:
choices: Assumes both governments had equal bargaining power
Assumes that what governments judge to be in their interest is in fact beneficial
Overlooks the interests of third countries
Ignores the role of domestic legislatures in ratification
questions.explanation: Correct: the argument slides from what each government judged to be in its interest to the agreement actually being beneficial, and governments misjudge, act on partial information, or serve narrow constituencies. Ignoring legislatures concerns the ratification process rather than the merits. Unequal bargaining power would explain a lopsided deal, which is a different objection and one that concedes the inference's form. Overlooking third countries widens the circle of affected parties without addressing the leap from judgment to fact.

questions.stem: The proposed measure assumes that:
choices: Embassies would conclude more agreements if their totals were published
The number of agreements concluded reflects the value of an embassy's work
Agreements are always implemented after being concluded
All embassies have equal opportunity to conclude agreements
questions.explanation: Correct: a count measures effectiveness only if what it counts tracks what it is meant to capture, so the whole proposal rests on agreements standing in for value — an embassy that averts a crisis or protects citizens in distress scores nothing at all. Requiring equal opportunity across every post is stronger than the proposal needs; it survives modest variation and fails only where the variation swamps performance. Whether agreements are implemented bears on what they are worth once signed, which the proposal never counts. Whether publishing totals would change behavior predicts a response to the metric rather than naming something it presupposes.

questions.stem: The evaluation's comparison is unreliable because:
choices: Villages able to contribute 20 percent of costs likely differ in wealth and organization
The project period was too short
Non-participating villages may have received other assistance
Sanitation outcomes were self-reported
questions.explanation: Correct: a 20 percent local contribution is a filter, and villages that can raise it are wealthier and better organized — advantages that improve sanitation on their own, so the outcome gap may have existed before the project began. Self-reported outcomes add noise to both groups alike. A short project period would tend to hide an effect rather than create one. Non-participating villages receiving other assistance would narrow the gap, making the finding harder to obtain rather than explaining it away.

questions.stem: The analyst's argument is flawed because the polls:
choices: Sample a population selected in a way that guarantees a favorable result
Do not report a margin of error
Were conducted too far before the election
May have been conducted by inexperienced staff
questions.explanation: Correct: the respondents came to the party's own website to register a preference, so the poll surveys the party's supporters and would show a lead however the wider electorate leans — the sample is built from the conclusion. Timing before the election concerns how much can change. A missing margin of error omits a standard disclosure. Inexperienced staff raise a question about execution, whereas this poll would be misleading if run flawlessly.

questions.stem: The official's argument assumes that:
choices: Holding the required certification indicates sufficient practical language ability
All officers wish to serve in language-designated positions
The certification examination is administered annually
Language training is the department's largest training expense
questions.explanation: Correct: the argument treats certification as proof of capability, so it holds only if the credential reflects usable ability — a certificate earned years ago, or on a test that rewards recall over conversation, would leave the 94 percent hollow. Officers wishing to serve in those positions concerns assignment preferences. The examination being annual is a scheduling detail. Language training being the largest training expense speaks to its cost rather than to whether the certification measures what the official claims.

questions.stem: The researcher's conclusion is questionable because:
choices: Climate risk is difficult to measure
Some exposed countries are also vocal
Vocal advocacy is not the same as effective advocacy
States may pursue interests other than direct physical exposure, such as commercial or reputational advantage
questions.explanation: Correct: self-interest is broader than physical exposure — a state may seek export markets in green technology, leverage over other states, or standing with its public — so low exposure does not clear the motive. Climate risk being hard to measure questions how exposure was ranked. Advocacy not being effective concerns its results rather than its motives. Some exposed countries also being vocal notes an overlap that leaves the researcher's inference about the unexposed ones untouched.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the evaluator's observation?
choices: Audits should never be required of grantees
The donor should fund only large organizations
The audit requirement screens on organizational size rather than on merit
Small organizations are less accountable than large ones
questions.explanation: Correct: the requirement admits organizations by their ability to pay for an audit, and that ability tracks size rather than how well they use money, so the filter selects on the wrong attribute. Saying audits should never be required prescribes a remedy the observation does not warrant. Saying small organizations are less accountable inverts the point, since the difficulty is affording the proof rather than lacking the discipline. Saying the donor should fund only large organizations endorses the very effect being criticised.

questions.stem: The commentator's argument confuses:
choices: Multilateral with unilateral sanctions
The imposition of costs with the achievement of the policy objective
Economic damage with humanitarian harm
Short-term with long-term effects
questions.explanation: Correct: sanctions are meant to change behavior, so damage inflicted is the instrument rather than the objective — a target can be badly hurt and still concede nothing. Confusing economic damage with humanitarian harm concerns who bears the cost, which is a moral question rather than the logical slip here. Distinguishing multilateral from unilateral sanctions classifies the measure. Confusing short- with long-term effects concerns timing, and the argument would fail on the same ground at any horizon.

questions.stem: The officer's argument is flawed because it:
choices: Assumes family connections are always disclosed
Relies on an unverified claim about the connections
Attacks the source of the assessment rather than its substance
Overlooks the colleague's professional record
questions.explanation: Correct: the assessment stands or falls on its evidence and reasoning, and pointing to who wrote it substitutes a fact about the analyst for an examination of the analysis. Assuming connections are always disclosed concerns the process for identifying them. Overlooking the professional record offers a counterweight of the same defective kind, weighing the person rather than the argument. Calling the claim about the connections unverified disputes whether the premise is true, whereas the argument would still be flawed if it were.

questions.stem: The change in survey method matters because:
choices: Telephone surveys are always less accurate
Differences in mode can shift responses independently of any change in actual trust
Respondents may have forgotten the initiative
The sample size may have changed
questions.explanation: Correct: people answer a stranger on the telephone differently from one across a table, and that mode effect can produce a 9-point move with no change in what anyone actually thinks — the two surveys are not measuring on the same instrument. Saying telephone surveys are always less accurate overstates a general claim and still would not explain a directional shift. A changed sample size affects precision rather than level. Respondents forgetting the initiative concerns their awareness, not the comparison between two differently administered surveys.

questions.stem: The specialist's argument is most vulnerable to the objection that:
choices: The organization has other functions besides preventing war
The organization's membership has changed over time
The war preceding the organization's founding may explain the subsequent peace
Member states have had disputes short of war
questions.explanation: Correct: a decisive war that settled the territorial questions removes the thing members would fight over, so the peace may be the war's legacy and the organization merely its contemporary. The organization having other functions concerns its broader value. Disputes short of war refine the description of the peace without explaining its cause. Membership changing over time complicates the comparison across years, but the founding settlement would account for the pattern regardless.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most undermine the official's proposal?
choices: Programs should be evaluated by what they accomplish rather than by what they cost to administer
Grant decisions should be made by technical experts
Administrative costs should be minimized wherever possible
Donors should support a diverse portfolio of grantees
questions.explanation: Correct: the proposal rests entirely on administrative cost, so a principle that subordinates cost to accomplishment attacks its foundation and reopens the possibility that small grants earn their overhead. Minimising administrative costs restates the official's own premise. Leaving grant decisions to technical experts concerns who decides rather than on what basis. Supporting a diverse portfolio would favor keeping small grants, but it argues from breadth as a value in itself rather than engaging the cost-versus-accomplishment trade the proposal turns on.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most support the commentator's conclusion?
choices: A program should be judged a failure unless rigorous evaluation demonstrates a measurable benefit
Programs should be continued until proven harmful
Household income is the best measure of development impact
Evaluation methods should be chosen by independent experts
questions.explanation: Correct: the commentator moves from no demonstrated benefit to failure, which needs a principle putting the burden of proof on the program and treating an undemonstrated benefit as none. Continuing programs until proven harmful places the burden on the other side and would rescue the program. Letting independent experts choose evaluation methods concerns procedure. Making household income the best measure of impact defends the outcome chosen, yet even the best measure showing nothing does not by itself license the verdict.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most support the official's proposal?
choices: Career satisfaction should be measured annually
Personnel policies should maximize aggregate career satisfaction even where individual preferences differ
Hardship posts should receive additional resources
Officers should be consulted before assignment policies change
questions.explanation: Correct: the proposal compels officers who did not choose hardship service, so it needs a principle that lets an aggregate gain override individual preference — without it, the satisfaction finding cannot justify a mandate. Consulting officers before policy changes is a procedural safeguard that cuts the other way. Giving hardship posts additional resources addresses conditions at those posts. Measuring satisfaction annually improves the data rather than justifying the requirement built on it.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the director's conclusion?
choices: The institute has operated for twenty years
The certification examination is nationally standardized
Among applicants with identical admission scores, those admitted outperform those turned away
Graduates report high satisfaction with the curriculum
questions.explanation: Correct: comparing admitted and rejected applicants at identical admission scores holds prior ability fixed, so a remaining gap is attributable to the institute rather than to who got in. Twenty years of operation establishes longevity. Graduates reporting satisfaction measures their opinion of the curriculum rather than its effect. A nationally standardised examination makes the outcome measure consistent, which is useful but leaves the selection problem entirely in place.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best supported by the exchange described?
choices: The necessity of the program has not been established by the evidence cited
Conventional methods are always sufficient
The security service acted unlawfully
The surveillance program disrupted no plots
questions.explanation: Correct: the group does not dispute the four disruptions; it points out that the evidence cannot distinguish a necessary program from a redundant one, so necessity remains unshown either way. Saying the program disrupted no plots contradicts the premise both sides accept. Saying conventional methods are always sufficient is a sweeping claim the group carefully avoids making. Saying the service acted unlawfully imports a legal verdict that the exchange, which is about justification, never reaches.

questions.stem: The economic section's argument depends on the assumption that:
choices: The host government has a motive to misreport
International organizations have questioned the figures
Other economies in the region report lower growth
Genuine growth in an economy of this kind would show more year-to-year variation
questions.explanation: Correct: the inference from smoothness to unreliability works only if real growth in such an economy would move around more; if genuine figures could sit that flat, the observation loses its force entirely. A motive to misreport would help explain falsification but is not needed to conclude the numbers look implausible. Regional economies reporting lower growth compares levels rather than variability. International organizations questioning the figures would be corroboration from outside rather than a premise the argument rests on.

questions.stem: Which of the following must be true if the evaluator's observation is accurate?
choices: The donor is indifferent to local rootedness
Audited organizations perform better than unaudited ones
Some organizations capable of performing well are excluded from funding by the audit requirement
Audit costs exceed the value of small grants
questions.explanation: Correct: the requirement excludes organizations that cannot afford audits, and affordability is unrelated to competence, so among those excluded there will be some that would have performed well. Saying audited organizations perform better asserts a link the observation never establishes. Saying the donor is indifferent to local rootedness reads an attitude into a rule that may have been adopted for unrelated reasons. Saying audit costs exceed the value of small grants compares two figures neither of which is given.

questions.stem: If both the ministry's figure and the registration figure are accurate, which is best supported?
choices: Traffic fatalities will rise again next year
The campaign had no effect whatsoever
Fatalities per registered vehicle did not fall and may have risen
The fuel price increase was intended as a safety measure
questions.explanation: Correct: exposure fell further than deaths — 22 percent against 18 — so per registered vehicle the fatality rate held steady at best and more likely worsened, which is the opposite of what the campaign claims. Saying the campaign had no effect whatsoever overstates it; a modest effect could be hidden inside these figures. Saying the fuel price increase was intended as a safety measure attributes a purpose the stimulus does not give. Predicting a rise next year forecasts beyond anything the two figures support.
